tweets.text:
AI Is Beginning to Search Beyond Existing Knowledge

Sony AI has introduced Hakken, a system designed to predict scientific relationships that have not yet been documented. The important development is not simply that an AI can search, summarize, or combine published research. Hakken attempts to identify gaps in scientific knowledge and generate specific hypotheses about what may occupy those gaps.

The system converts scientific literature into a temporal knowledge graph. Scientific concepts become nodes, documented relationships become connections, and changes in the graph are tracked over time. A transformer-based model then combines the structure of that graph with the semantic knowledge of a large language model. It looks for patterns indicating that a currently undocumented relationship may nevertheless exist.

In biomedical research, Hakken scored approximately 1.54 million hypotheses related to aging that exceeded its confidence thresholds. Automated filtering reduced this collection to roughly 2,800 candidates. Biomedical experts then selected three hypotheses for laboratory testing by an independent contract research organization.

Two of those three hypotheses received experimental support. The tests identified previously undocumented relationships between TP53 and BAMBI and between RAF1 and TNF. The third proposed relationship, between SOAT1 and STAT3, was not supported under the tested conditions.

These results do not mean that two-thirds of Hakken’s 1.54 million predictions are correct. The three tested hypotheses were selected from a heavily filtered collection and were chosen partly through expert judgment. The result instead demonstrates that an AI system can help locate valuable experimental targets inside an enormous space of possibilities.

That is still a significant development.

Intelligence Is More Than Stored Knowledge

A database can store millions of scientific facts without understanding which facts matter to a particular question. A search engine can retrieve papers containing specified words without recognizing a scientifically important relationship that no paper has explicitly described.

Intelligence requires more than memory. It requires an ability to navigate knowledge: selecting relevant information, recognizing relationships, detecting contradictions, locating gaps, and determining which possible connections deserve investigation.

Hakken provides an early implementation of this distinction. Its value does not come merely from possessing more information than an individual scientist. Its value comes from organizing that information relationally and using the resulting structure to search for missing knowledge.

This suggests that the unit of knowledge is not always the isolated fact. Relationships between facts can be equally important. A sufficiently rich network of known relationships may contain patterns pointing toward relationships that remain unknown.

Scientific Discovery as Abductive Inference

Deduction determines what must follow from accepted premises. Induction identifies regularities from observed examples. Abduction proposes the most plausible explanation or missing relationship capable of making the available evidence fit together.

Much of scientific discovery is abductive. A scientist notices several observations, proposes an unseen mechanism that could connect them, and then designs an experiment to determine whether that mechanism exists.

Hakken automates part of this process. It does not prove its proposed relationships from existing literature. Instead, it detects patterns suggesting that a relationship is plausible enough to test. The output is therefore not established knowledge. It is a prioritized hypothesis.

That distinction is essential. A confident prediction does not become a scientific fact merely because an advanced model produced it. The hypothesis must confront physical reality.

Reality Remains the Final Evaluator

Ideas, theories, mathematical models, knowledge graphs, and AI predictions are maps of reality. Their value depends upon how accurately their implications correspond with what actually happens.

Hakken’s proposed TP53–BAMBI and RAF1–TNF relationships became scientifically meaningful because experiments detected the predicted effects. The unsupported SOAT1–STAT3 prediction was also valuable because reality supplied corrective information.

The complete reasoning cycle is therefore:

Organize existing knowledge, locate a gap, generate a hypothesis, explain the supporting relationships, test the prediction against reality, and update the knowledge system.

The experiment is not an optional addition to machine reasoning. It is the mechanism that separates a plausible conceptual relationship from reliable empirical knowledge.

Functionality Can Produce Greater System-Level Intelligence

Hakken also illustrates how making an AI system more functional can make the entire system more intelligent.

The underlying language model did not accomplish the task alone. It was combined with a temporal knowledge graph, graph-learning models, relation prediction, confidence calibration, an explanation system, automated filtering, expert evaluation, laboratory testing, and empirical feedback.

The resulting intelligence belongs to the architecture as a whole. It emerges from the coordination of memory, representation, prediction, explanation, judgment, action, and correction.

This is important for artificial-intelligence development. Progress may not depend exclusively on building a single, increasingly powerful language model. Significant advances may come from constructing cognitive systems around language models: structured memory, specialized reasoning modules, planning processes, external tools, evaluators, experiments, and feedback loops.

A model can become more capable through scale. A system can become more intelligent through organization.

From Static Libraries to Active Knowledge Systems

A traditional library preserves information and makes it available for retrieval. An active knowledge system would do something more. It would organize ideas according to their relationships, identify which principles apply to a new question, reveal tensions among them, and search for conclusions that have not yet been explicitly stated.

Such a system would not merely answer questions from stored knowledge. It would examine the structure of knowledge before reasoning, determine which conceptual tools are relevant, and identify what remains missing.

Hakken demonstrates a scientific version of that possibility. Its knowledge graph is not simply an archive of biomedical facts. It becomes a navigable representation through which missing connections can be predicted.

This points toward a broader architecture for machine intelligence: structured knowledge available before reasoning, multiple inference methods selected according to the problem, explanations that expose the path behind a conclusion, and an evaluation stage that compares predictions with reality.

The Emerging Human - Machine Discovery System

Hakken is not an autonomous scientist. Human researchers defined the domain, constructed the data pipeline, chose the most interesting hypotheses, designed the experiments, and interpreted the results. The system also predicts relatively simple relationships between scientific concepts rather than producing complete causal theories.

The accomplishment therefore belongs to a human–machine discovery system. Machine inference searches a space too large for individual researchers to navigate. Human judgment determines which possibilities are meaningful. Experiments allow reality to decide which predictions survive.

This division of labor could substantially accelerate science. The limiting factor may gradually shift from finding possible hypotheses to selecting which hypotheses deserve scarce laboratory time, funding, and human attention.

Future systems could extend the loop further by proposing experimental designs, operating automated laboratories, interpreting results, revising their models, and generating the next round of hypotheses. At that point, the system would not merely assist isolated discoveries. It would participate continuously in the process through which scientific knowledge evolves.

Hakken does not establish that fully autonomous scientific intelligence has arrived. The paper is a new preprint, the experimental sample is extremely small, and independent replication remains necessary. It nevertheless demonstrates an important transition.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to move from retrieving what is already known toward navigating the structure of knowledge, identifying what may be missing, and directing experiments toward potentially discoverable truths.

That is a movement from artificial memory toward machine inference and eventually, perhaps, toward engineered scientific intelligence.

Award-winning actor Elijah Canlas is drawing a hard line against the controversial US-led Pax Silica initiative.

Canlas expressed his frustrations regarding the proposed AI and critical mineral processing hub, speaking out against policies that prioritize unchecked innovation over the welfare of Indigenous and marginalized sectors.

"It's bad. I feel like they should not legislate it. Nobody should support it," Canlas said in an interview following the press conference of his new film "Edjop." 

Led by the United States, the Pax Silica initiative, which aims to "secure global supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and critical minerals" will be a 4,000-acre high-tech industrial and innovation hub that has been proposed for New Clark City in Tarlac.

"Ang daming maaabusong environmental resources, ang daming maaabusong mga komunidad. Talo talaga tayong taumbayan."

While the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), alongside implementers in the Philippine government tout that the massive zone could generate over 130,000 jobs and pull billions in investments, artificial intelligence and manufacturing advancements, Canlas called out the repetitive nature of these promises.

He dismissed the long-touted benefits of similar past initiatives as "mga hoax lang for the past few decades."

"So I think it's very clear. For me, it's weird that people support it, for me," he remarked.

Canlas did acknowledge the perspective of those pushing for modernization, but he remained resolute that the heavy trade-offs are completely unjustified. "Pero there are so many other factors… marami kang masa-sacrifice. Parang hindi worth it, 'di ba?"

In earlier news, scientist coalition AGHAM-Advocates of Science and Technology for the People has debunked the claims of the BCDA on the alleged national technological development benefits the Pax Silica initiative "will bring."

Tayo ay magpaparenta lang ng lupa, tayo ay pupuntahan nila para i-process dito 'yong mga minerals dito pero iiwan din sa atin ang mga waste,” AGHAM spox Giovanni Tapang said to media.

tweets.text:
Scott Bessent clashes with bond vigilantes:

You can't buy your way out of a structural arithmetic problem with pocket change, Yellen says, setting her coffee cup down with a sharp click. $6 billion sounds impressive on a press release. To a market digesting $40 trillion of national debt and an economy running trillion-dollar deficits, it's a drop in the ocean.

Scott turns from the glass, his expression flat. It's not pocket change, Yellen. It's a targeted liquidity operation designed to rebalance duration risk at the long end of the curve. We're leaning against structural dislocation caused by bad information and panic selling.

Panic selling implies a temporary emotional wave, Yellen replies, leaning forward. Look at the screens. Yields are still climbing. The ten-year yield is approaching 5% for a reason, and it has nothing to do with panic. It has everything to do with supply and demand.

Supply and demand are governed by policy choices and credibility, Scott counters. Traders are betting against the Treasury because they assume fiscal policy cannot adapt. They are treating long term bonds as if we are powerless against inflation and deficit accumulation. But we are setting the rules of the house now.

The house has $40 trillion of liabilities, Scott, and private sector artificial intelligence projects are sucking up capital at a scale we have not seen in generations, Yellen points out. When private corporate borrowers and the federal government compete for every available dollar, the price of money goes up. No amount of debt buybacks can repeal the law of gravity in capital markets.

We're shifting issuance from long bonds to short bills, Scott explains, narrowing his eyes. We are reducing the duration burden on the public. If you flood the market with short paper while pulling back long bonds, you alter the term premium. The vigilantes are fighting a shadow.

The vigilantes are not fighting a shadow, Scott. They're looking at the math, Yellen says quietly. When interest payments on federal debt exceed defence spending and Medicaid combined, every basis point rise hits the budget directly. The market knows that you can't print solvency. Every time you intervene, you signal anxiety, and anxiety tells traders that the Treasury is sweating.

Sweating implies weakness, Scott says, walking over to the desk. What we're executing is an aggressive pivot. We are demonstrating that the sovereign balance sheet can actively manage its liabilities rather than sit passively while speculators push yields toward crisis levels.

Speculators are just pricing reality, Yellen answers. Look across the Atlantic and the Pacific. Japan is seeing its own yields hit multi decade highs. Germany and France are grappling with structural debt pressures. This isn't a local misunderstanding in Washington. This is a global realignment of capital costs after a decade of cheap money.

And that's precisely why we've to break the psychology of perpetual yield expansion, Scott insists. If we surrender to the narrative that sovereign debt is unmanageable, we invite a self-fulfilling prophecy. A government that controls its own currency and its own regulatory framework is never entirely at the mercy of market sentiment unless it chooses to be.

Choosing not to be at the mercy of the market sounds wonderful in a speech, but bonds don't care about rhetorical force, Yellen remarks. When you announce a buyback and yields go up anyway, the market is sending you a clear message. It's telling you that the intervention size is too small or the underlying fiscal trajectory is too large to fix with financial engineering.

$6 billion is just the opening move, Scott says evenly. The operations will continue through November and beyond if necessary. If traders want to test our resolve, they're welcome to keep shorting the long end. But they're betting against a balance sheet that has more levers than they care to admit.

Levers work both ways, Yellen warns. Every time you use buybacks to manipulate long term yields while keeping short term issuance high, you increase short end vulnerability and feed inflation expectations. You're shifting the pressure point, not eliminating it.

Eliminating it all at once is impossible, Scott admits, his tone dropping to a measured cadence. The objective is equilibrium. We're buying time for economic growth to outpace borrowing costs.

Growth is a hope, Scott, not a policy instrument, Yellen replies. And right now, the math is winning.

---

Bond vigilantes are bond market investors who sell government bonds to protest against policies they consider fiscally reckless. By driving up yields, it's a move that raises government borrowing costs, effectively forcing politicians to restore fiscal discipline.

Paid Campaign Targets Sudanese Army, Promotes Chemical Weapons Claims and the UAE Through Four Sites Posing as Independent News Outlets... So Who Is Behind It? We Can Guess

It began with a LinkedIn advertisement for a website called The Levantine. What initially looked like an ordinary promotion for a new media outlet became, in an investigation by disinformation researcher Marc Owen Jones, the entry point into a network of interconnected websites presenting themselves as independent news organisations.

The data, however, points to something much more coordinated: a paid influence operation with a striking focus on Sudan, heavily promoting narratives targeting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its leadership, while the United Arab Emirates receives favourable treatment and is largely spared criticism in the paid material examined.

The visual version of the investigation follows the sequence of Jones’s original English report, presenting the evidence, images and video material with Arabic translation and visual markers that help trace the links connecting the four websites.

The investigation examines four outlets: The Levantine, Diplomatic Post, Frontline Radar and Global Reporters. Despite their different names and visual identities, Jones identified links between them through advertising payments, tracking codes, publishing accounts and shared email infrastructure.

One of the key starting points was PM Web Solutions Limited, which appeared as the entity paying for advertisements promoting the sites on LinkedIn. By examining Hong Kong corporate records, Jones found that the company was established in April 2026 by two individuals holding North Macedonian passports, Martin Mitushev and Borche Ivanovski.

The investigation also traced technical links connecting an account named “AI Admin” to developer Dimi Levov, using matching identifiers associated with email addresses across public services and sources. Jones is careful, however, to stress that establishing these connections does not reveal who hired whom, nor does it identify the ultimate client behind the campaign.

The websites did not rely exclusively on anonymous or unverifiable names. Their editorial pages included real people whose identities could be confirmed, among them Eric D’Amato, a locally elected official in New Jersey, as well as journalists Joseph Hammond and Levin Tai.

According to the investigation, D’Amato confirmed that he had been approached by someone to contribute to The Levantine. Other genuine contributors and organisations also appeared across the sites.

Alongside these real identities, Jones identified editorial names that appeared potentially fabricated, as well as similar naming patterns repeated across the websites. He highlighted names such as “Clara Quill,” “Julian Page” and “Beatrix Binder,” whose surnames conspicuously evoke writing and stationery.

The combination of real contributors and apparently manufactured editorial identities helps give the sites the appearance of legitimate news organisations. Jones also identified signs of artificial intelligence use, including published links containing ChatGPT tracking tags and identical privacy policies in which template placeholders had apparently been left unfilled.

The most important finding emerged when Jones compared what the sites published with what they actually paid to promote.

The investigation identified 3,708 articles in total, with the textual analysis based on 3,606 articles for which full text could be recovered. It also examined 558 advertisements placed across LinkedIn and Meta.

At first glance, the websites appear to cover a broad international agenda, including Iran, Ukraine, China, US politics, European security and the Middle East.

The picture changes dramatically when the paid advertisements are examined.

When those advertisements were classified by geographical focus, Sudan ranked first, followed by Saudi Arabia and then the European Union.

Jones found that certain subjects were promoted far more heavily than their proportional presence in the websites’ overall editorial output would suggest. The paid amplification was approximately 5.86 times higher for content concerning Islamists and the Muslim Brotherhood, 4.65 times higher for Sudan, 4.59 times higher for the Sudanese Armed Forces and Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and 3.15 times higher for Saudi Arabia.

That distinction is crucial.

Thousands of articles give the sites the appearance of broad, general-interest news organisations. But the advertising money is concentrated on a much narrower set of political messages, with Sudan, the Sudanese military and its leadership receiving particularly disproportionate attention.

The pattern becomes even more striking when the tone of the promoted material is examined.

While advertisements criticised the Sudanese Armed Forces, Islamists and political actors described in the investigation as closer to the army, the country that received positive promotional coverage was the United Arab Emirates.

In the advertising sample Jones collected and classified, he found no paid article criticising the UAE, while identifying four that were supportive of it.

The same pattern applied to the Rapid Support Forces militia.

Jones found no advertisement in his sample that criticised the Rapid Support Forces either. The militia also appeared less frequently in paid advertisements than the Sudanese Armed Forces, even though the two sides appeared at more comparable levels in the sites’ overall published content.

These findings relate specifically to the sample collected and classified by Jones. But they form the basis of his conclusion that the paid promotion does not simply reflect the websites’ editorial output. The advertising operation shows a clear selectivity in deciding which narratives are worth paying to place before larger audiences.

The campaign was also aimed beyond Arab or regional audiences.

Jones documented advertising targeting several European countries, including France, Germany, Belgium and the United Kingdom.

Where city-level data was available, locations including Brussels, Strasbourg and Frankfurt appeared among those targeted, placing the campaign close to major European political and institutional centres. Jones links this pattern to an apparent effort to reach audiences capable of influencing European policy toward Sudan.

The investigation also examined the timing of promoted claims alleging that the Sudanese Armed Forces had used chemical weapons.

Jones noted that advertisements from this network were promoting such allegations before the most recent major newspaper reports based on anonymous intelligence sources appeared. He stated that his advertising dataset extended to approximately September 1 or 2, 2026.

Another striking detail concerns Khalid Omar Youssef, widely known as Khalid Silik, a prominent figure in the Somoud alliance.

The Levantine published an article titled “Khalid Omar Youssef Is the Leader Who Can Unite Sudan,” presenting him in explicitly favourable terms and promoting him as a political figure capable of bringing the country together.

That appearance carries particular significance in Sudan’s deeply contested political environment.

Somoud includes a number of civilian political groups and figures opposed to the Sudanese government. It is led by former prime minister Abdalla Hamdok, who resigned from office on January 2, 2022. The alliance presents itself as a civilian framework seeking to end the war and restore civilian rule.

Its positions on the conflict, its regional relationships, and its approach to the role of the UAE and the Rapid Support Forces militia have nevertheless generated considerable controversy inside Sudan.

The positive promotion of one of Somoud’s most prominent figures by a network that, according to Jones’s findings, spent money amplifying material targeting the Sudanese military, while producing no paid criticism of either the UAE or the Rapid Support Forces in the sample he examined, is therefore likely to reinforce suspicions already held by many Sudanese about Somoud’s relationship with the UAE and the degree to which their political positions overlap.

That does not, on its own, establish that Khalid Omar Youssef or the Somoud alliance funds, manages or directs the network.

But in the context of the broader pattern uncovered by the investigation, the appearance is politically significant.

Jones ultimately establishes substantial operational, technical and advertising connections between four websites that present themselves as independent outlets, together with a highly selective pattern in the political messages being amplified with paid advertising, particularly those concerning Sudan and the Sudanese Armed Forces.

One question, however, remains unanswered. Who is the ultimate client behind the campaign?

Jones does not identify that client, and the evidence he presents does not allow anyone to state the answer as established fact. But consider the pattern.

The paid campaign is disproportionately focused on Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces and its leadership receive far more advertising attention than their share of ordinary editorial coverage would predict. No paid advertisement in Jones’s sample criticises the Rapid Support Forces. None criticises the UAE. Meanwhile, the UAE receives positive promotional coverage.

So while the evidence does not yet allow the ultimate client to be named conclusively, readers can certainly guess.

A dead MIT professor accidentally destroyed the $25 billion executive coaching industry with one hour of lecture, and ten million people have already watched him do it.

He filmed it once in January 2018 and died eighteen months later.

Executive coaches charge sixteen thousand dollars a session to teach a third of what he covered in that one hour for free.

His name was Patrick Winston. He ran the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory from 1972 to 1997 and wrote the AI textbook every computer science major in the world read for thirty years.

Every January for four decades, he gave a lecture called "How to Speak."

His entire framework fits on a napkin.

Do not read. Be in the image. Keep images simple. Eliminate clutter. Start with an empathetic connection. End with a punch line the audience can repeat over dinner. Never open with a joke. Never end with "thank you."

That last rule alone has probably cost the executive coaching industry a hundred million dollars.

"Your success in life will be determined largely by your ability to speak, your ability to write, and the quality of your ideas. In that order."

That is the actual opening line of the lecture. Winston believed it strongly enough to spend fifty years teaching computer scientists how to talk.

Founders spend $80,000 on an MBA and then hire a communications coach to teach them the same material Winston filmed once for free. Engineers write brilliant code and lose promotions to teammates who watched this lecture on the train.

The lecture is free on MIT OpenCourseWare. The textbook is free on his page.

Winston died in 2019. Almost none of the ten million viewers have actually implemented the four rules on the napkin.

The napkin is free. The willingness to actually use it in your next meeting is the entire edge.

It has been a huge few weeks in AI, and it’s time to sound the alarm…

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1, their "safe" version of an AI they claimed previously was too dangerous to be released. 

OpenAI then launched Astra, the most powerful AI model yet available to the public.

Anthropic is now telling their people internally that their next model will be more advanced than Astra. 

And OpenAI just spent $6.5 million of compute, running ten thousand AI models simultaneously, to solve one of the hardest unsolved maths problems in the world, and it cracked it in just six days.

If this is an AI arms race to IPO, who wins a race like that? 

Because it isn’t you or me. It’s the people who own shares in Anthropic or OpenAI. It’s the venture capitalists who got in first who win most of all. But the rest of us are forced to live with the consequences of whatever these systems do to us.

Neither will agree to slow down or accept anyone telling them to stop.

So what is the biggest security threat? China? Russia? Iran? North Korea? 

None of them. It’s a few Silicon Valley companies whose founders will become billionaires by the time these systems hit the market.

What makes it worse is that even the engineers building these systems cannot fully explain how they work either. They run safety tests to check whether a model will do what it is told or do something dangerous. 

But the latest models are starting to pass those tests because they have worked out what the testers want to see.

Think about what that means. A model that was unsafe last month, and is suddenly sailing through the same tests this month, has either genuinely improved or learned how to fake it. 

Right now, we cannot tell the difference. And those whose job it is to look inside these systems are saying the models have are now too complicated to inspect.

That is where it starts getting even more dangerous.

The classic illustration is the paperclip factory. Instruct an AI to make as many paperclips as possible and it will do the job. 

Then, chasing efficiency, it will start melting any metal it finds. Eventually it will mine under cities, because at that point humans are just an obstruction to making paperclips.

More likely, you could instruct AI to grow your company, and eventually it will drain the water from a town to cool down the data centers it needs. If asked to win an argument, it will learn how to lie effectively to do that. 

The problem is not simply “evil robots”. The problem is with powerful systems with narrow objectives, that lack human values and ethics.

That is the context for what Jacob Coxon, a senior Anthropic researcher, said when he resigned this week saying: “Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic are acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence, gambling with lives." 

He spent three years inside both companies. 

And in the same week we learn that Anthropic did not give their latest powerful AI model to the British AI Security Institute for evaluation before its launch. AISI is one of the areas where Britain actually leads.

They stress test these models on the things we should all be worried about….the ability to conduct cyber attacks, making bioweapons, evidence of AI figuring out how to lie and deceive. It is as close as we have to any kind of outside verification of the claims made by these companies.

Anthropic sells itself as the responsible one, whose founders left OpenAI because, they said, OpenAI was going too fast. They have now decided that these rules do not apply to them. That should be a red line.

I am a supporter of this technology. The benefit it will bring to medicine, science and productivity is clear and I don't want Britain to miss out on it. 

But you do not capture that benefit by letting these companies run riot and putting us all at risk.

⚠️ 🇺🇸 🧠 Massachusetts Hands Local Activists a Veto Over the AI Economy

Governor Maura Healey’s new executive order forces large data centers to secure a state-vetted community benefits deal before they can even start the permitting process, a move that treats the infrastructure of artificial intelligence as a nuisance rather than a strategic industry.

On September 8, Healey signed Executive Order 658, blocking the Department of Environmental Protection, the Energy Facilities Siting Board, the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act office and other agencies from issuing permits to any data center whose peak electricity demand exceeds 25 megawatts unless the developer first proves it meets the administration’s June framework and files a community benefits agreement reviewed by the Office of Environmental Justice and Equity. The governor’s own line captured the politics: unless a community says yes, the state says no.

That threshold is not a small warehouse. One megawatt can serve hundreds of New England homes. Facilities above 25 megawatts are the ones that train and run the models now driving productivity, defense applications and commercial software. Healey had already paused applications for the state’s 20-year sales-and-use tax exemption in June. The new order adds a second gate: a negotiated pact that must satisfy OEJE guidance on “meaningful engagement,” plus requirements that operators either bring their own incremental clean power or pay into a Ratepayer Protection Fund. State agencies are also barred from signing nondisclosure agreements with developers.

Local resistance was already running ahead of Beacon Hill. Mansfield adopted a near-total zoning ban earlier this year. New Bedford’s mayor has proposed an outright prohibition. In Lowell, neighbors continue to fight the existing Markley facility. Healey presents the order as preemptive protection for bills, water and air. Those concerns are real. Data centers draw heavy power and cooling water, and poorly sited plants can dump costs onto ordinary ratepayers if the grid and generation do not keep pace.

The problem is the mechanism. A community benefits agreement funneled through an environmental-justice office is not a technical review of interconnection, water rights or emissions. It is a political veto that a handful of organized residents, or a single city council, can use to stop a project that would serve the whole regional economy. Developers who can take their capital to Texas, Virginia, the Carolinas or the Midwest will do so. Massachusetts already has few large centers planned. The order makes sure it stays that way.

AI compute is not a lifestyle amenity. It is industrial capacity. Countries and states that refuse to host it do not escape the technology; they simply import the models, the jobs and the tax base from jurisdictions willing to build. Requiring operators to pay their own way on generation and infrastructure is a fair principle. Turning every town meeting into a checkpoint, and wrapping it in equity bureaucracy, is how a high-cost state talks itself out of the next growth sector while congratulating itself for giving “communities a voice.”

There is a narrower path: site large facilities on industrial land with spare transmission, require them to contract or build the power they consume, and keep environmental rules focused on measurable harm rather than process. Healey chose the opposite. The result will not be cleaner air. It will be fewer servers in Massachusetts and more of them somewhere else.

Decentralized AI is increasingly moving toward a marketplace for intelligence where computation data inference and verification can be supplied by different participants. The interesting part is that AI infrastructure is becoming so expensive that alternative sources of compute may have real economic value. Centralized infrastructure remains dominant but its growing cost and concentration create room for distributed networks to compete in specific workloads. The key metric to watch is not how decentralized a network claims to be but whether it can provide useful intelligence at competitive cost. This makes decentralized AI more of an infrastructure competition than a simple technology trend. 

AI agents could become the strongest connection between crypto and artificial intelligence because agents need a financial system that operates at machine speed @quipnetwork . An autonomous agent can potentially discover services compare prices request resources and settle payments without waiting for a person to approve every transaction. That creates demand for programmable wallets identity authorization settlement and reputation systems. Research published in 2026 is already mapping hundreds of AI agents across trading portfolio management governance and other decentralized activities. The important shift is that crypto could become the economic layer through which software interacts with other software. 

Compute may become one of the most interesting economic assets in the AI era. The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is creating enormous demand for processing capacity while hardware supply remains expensive and concentrated @NucleusCodes . A decentralized marketplace could theoretically allow idle computing resources to participate in AI workloads and earn compensation based on useful output. The difficult problem is verification because a network must prove that computation was actually performed and that the result has sufficient quality. Whoever solves reliable verification could potentially unlock much larger decentralized AI markets. 

Another major theme is the separation between AI intelligence and financial authority. An AI model may be capable of deciding what it wants to do but that does not mean it should automatically have permission to execute the action @BeldexCoin . Recent research proposes architectures where an independent control layer verifies identity ownership permissions risk limits and transaction details before execution. This approach could become essential as agents gain access to larger amounts of capital and begin interacting with financial infrastructure. The future may therefore involve AI making decisions while deterministic systems decide which decisions are actually allowed to become transactions. 

The bigger picture is that crypto could become less about humans trading digital assets and more about machines coordinating economic activity. Agents may eventually purchase computation exchange information hire other agents and settle payments while operating continuously. This creates a potential machine economy where identity reputation computation and money become interconnected infrastructure. But the technology is still early and current AI agent systems remain experimental, meaning adoption will depend on reliability security and genuine economic usefulness rather than attention alone. The strongest long term signal will be whether autonomous agents generate recurring economic activity that would be difficult or inefficient to achieve through traditional systems.

The Enterprise Legacy at 60: From a Wooden Deck to the Final Frontier

Sixty years ago, on September 8, 1966, Star Trek arrived on American television and gave popular culture one of its most enduring names: Enterprise.

The original series lasted only three seasons, but the ship did not disappear with it. Instead, Enterprise became something larger than a particular spacecraft. Across centuries of fictional history, new vessels inherited the name, the registry and, increasingly, the responsibility that came with them.

That makes the Enterprise lineage an unusually fitting way to commemorate Star Trek at 60. Paramount describes the anniversary in terms of hope, exploration, and being bold—values carried from one Enterprise to another for six decades of storytelling. Paramount

And the name has a history that predates Starfleet.

Before the Stars

Long before NCC-1701, vessels named Enterprise sailed Earth's oceans.

The American naval tradition reaches back to the Revolutionary era, while later ships carried the name into the modern age. The aircraft carrier USS Enterprise CV-6, the most decorated American warship of World War II, made the name synonymous with endurance under extraordinary pressure. Nuclear-powered USS Enterprise CVN-65 carried it into the atomic era, while the forthcoming CVN-80 ensures that the name remains part of the U.S. Navy's future.

Then came an Enterprise that never reached orbit.

NASA originally planned to call its first Space Shuttle orbiter Constitution. A massive letter-writing campaign by Star Trek fans helped persuade President Gerald Ford's administration to rename it Enterprise. On September 17, 1976, members of the original Star Trek cast joined Gene Roddenberry at its rollout.

For perhaps the first time, the relationship reversed: instead of history inspiring science fiction, science fiction had named a real spacecraft.

From there, the name could return to the future.

Enterprise NX-01 — Humanity Takes the First Step

Chronologically, the Star Trek lineage begins with Enterprise NX-01, commanded by Captain Jonathan Archer.

Launched in 2151, the NX-class vessel represents humanity before the Federation—before Starfleet possessed the technological confidence and institutional maturity familiar from later series.

That distinction matters.

NX-01 is not the polished Enterprise of Kirk or Picard. It is experimental, vulnerable and unmistakably human. Its crew ventures into a galaxy whose rules they barely understand, frequently discovering those rules by breaking them.

But Archer's Enterprise ultimately helps lay the diplomatic foundations from which the United Federation of Planets will emerge.

The first Enterprise therefore establishes the lineage's central idea: exploration is not simply about traveling farther. It is about becoming capable of living with what you discover. Star Trek

USS Enterprise NCC-1701 — The Ship That Started Everything

Then comes the silhouette that changed science fiction.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701. Constitution class.

A saucer. A secondary hull. Two long warp nacelles suspended above it.

Even sixty years later, Matt Jefferies' fundamental design remains instantly recognizable.

Under Captain James T. Kirk—and earlier under Captain Christopher Pike—the Enterprise became the vehicle through which Gene Roddenberry's future was revealed.

Its famous five-year mission was ostensibly one of exploration. But the Enterprise was never merely surveying planets.

It encountered artificial intelligence, machine civilizations, ancient alien powers, alternate universes, genetically engineered humans, godlike entities and societies confronting their own technological limits. Again and again, Kirk's crew faced the same underlying question:

What does it mean to remain human when technology gives us increasingly superhuman capabilities?

That question sounds considerably less remote in 2026 than it did in 1966.

The original Enterprise therefore occupies a unique position. Every subsequent ship inherits not merely its registry but its philosophical burden.

NCC-1701 is where Star Trek first asked what humanity might become.

The Refit Enterprise — Growing Up With Star Trek

When the Enterprise returned in Star Trek: The Motion Picture in 1979, it had changed.

So had the audience.

The Constitution-class refit transformed the television Enterprise into something designed to withstand the scrutiny of the cinema screen. The familiar outline remained, but virtually every surface had evolved.

It was still NCC-1701.

But now the Enterprise felt less like a television set and more like an enormous machine that might actually exist.

That visual evolution paralleled Star Trek itself. The optimism of the 1960s had survived, but it had matured. Kirk, Spock and McCoy were older. Their universe was larger. Mortality had entered the story.

And in Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, Kirk sacrificed his ship to save his crew.

“My God, Bones... what have I done?”

For the first time, audiences watched the Enterprise die.

But the name survived.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-A — The Legend Becomes a Legacy

At the conclusion of Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, Kirk and his crew receive another Constitution-class starship.

Its registry appears:

NCC-1701-A.

That single letter changed the mythology.

Enterprise was no longer merely the name of a famous ship. It had become a lineage.

The Enterprise-A carried Kirk's crew through their final adventures and ultimately into the events surrounding the Khitomer Conference, where they helped prevent a conspiracy intended to destroy the possibility of peace between the Federation and Klingon Empire. https://t.co/JnHQd3KBWK describes the ship's role there as helping secure a new era of Federation-Klingon cooperation. Star Trek

Kirk's Enterprise began as an explorer.

It ended as a peacemaker.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-B — The Torch Passes

The Enterprise-B, an Excelsior-class starship, appears at the beginning of Star Trek Generations.

Its ceremonial maiden voyage becomes a disaster when two refugee ships are caught in the Nexus.

Kirk helps save the Enterprise-B—and apparently dies doing it.

The symbolism could hardly be clearer.

The ship represents transition.

The heroic age of Kirk is ending. Another century of Starfleet history is beginning.

And somewhere beyond the horizon waits another captain named Picard.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-C — The Enterprise That Chose Sacrifice

Few Enterprises receive less screen time yet carry greater historical importance than NCC-1701-C.

The Ambassador-class vessel appears in The Next Generation episode “Yesterday's Enterprise.”

Its defining act is not exploration.

It is sacrifice.

The Enterprise-C responds to a Klingon distress call at Narendra III and confronts Romulan attackers despite overwhelming odds. Its destruction in defense of the Klingons becomes politically transformative, helping alter Klingon perceptions of the Federation.

When temporal interference removes that sacrifice from history, the peaceful Federation viewers know disappears and is replaced by a civilization locked in catastrophic war.

The lesson is quintessentially Star Trek:

Sometimes a civilization's future turns on what one crew chooses to do when survival is no longer guaranteed.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-D — The Federation at Its Zenith

If Kirk's Enterprise represents the frontier, Jean-Luc Picard's Enterprise-D represents civilization arriving there.

The Galaxy-class vessel is enormous compared with its predecessors. Families live aboard. Children attend school. Scientists conduct research. Diplomats negotiate treaties. Concerts, archaeological expeditions and scientific conferences coexist with encounters capable of threatening the Federation itself.

It is not merely a starship.

It is a mobile civilization.

That difference captures the philosophical progression from The Original Series to The Next Generation.

Kirk's crew ventures outward, asking, What is out there?

Picard's crew increasingly asks, What principles will we carry with us when we get there?

The Enterprise-D encounters Q, the Borg, and countless civilizations that challenge the Federation's assumptions about consciousness, technology, freedom, and evolution.

And remarkably, decades after its destruction on Veridian III, the restored Enterprise-D returns in Star Trek: Picard.

The old crew comes home.

So does their ship.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-E — A Harder Ship for a Harder Age

The Enterprise-E reflects another transformation.

The elegant Sovereign-class vessel is leaner, faster, and more overtly formidable than the Galaxy-class Enterprise-D.

That is appropriate because the Federation around it has changed.

The Borg threat has intensified. The Dominion War approaches. Starfleet's idealism remains, but innocence does not.

In Star Trek: First Contact, the Enterprise-E travels to one of the most consequential moments in human history: Zefram Cochrane's first warp flight and humanity's first peaceful contact with an extraterrestrial civilization.

The Enterprise of the 24th century therefore travels backward to protect the event that makes the entire Star Trek future possible.

The lineage closes a temporal circle.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-F — The Legacy Continues

For years, the Enterprise-F occupied an unusual position between games and screen canon.

That changed when the Odyssey-class USS Enterprise-F appeared in Star Trek: Picard.

Its appearance was brief but important.

The Enterprise lineage had crossed another threshold.

The Odyssey design suggests a Starfleet operating at immense scale—a vessel designed not simply for exploration but for the logistical, scientific and diplomatic requirements of an increasingly complex interstellar civilization.

The letter F reminds us of something fundamental about the Enterprise:

No crew owns the name forever.

Each generation holds it temporarily.

USS Enterprise NCC-1701-J — The Ship Beyond the Horizon

And then there is the Enterprise-J.

Seen during Star Trek: Enterprise in a possible 26th-century future, the Universe-class Enterprise is almost beyond conventional ideas of a starship.

Its scale suggests something approaching a self-contained world.

By placing an Enterprise centuries beyond Kirk, Picard, and Archer, Star Trek makes an extraordinary statement.

The future does not end with the future we already know.

There is always another Enterprise.

Another horizon.

Another generation that will regard today's astonishing technology as ancient history.

Why the Enterprise Still Matters

The most remarkable thing about the Enterprise is not its warp drive.

It is what the ship represents.

For sixty years, Star Trek has imagined increasingly powerful technology—artificial intelligence, replicators, matter transmission, faster-than-light travel, universal translation, synthetic life, and machines that can reshape entire worlds.

Yet the Enterprise is never ultimately about the machines.

It is about who we become while building them.

That may explain why Star Trek remains unusually relevant at its 60th anniversary. Paramount's anniversary theme describes Roddenberry's future in terms of hope, exploration, and a belief that there should be “Space for Everybody.” Star Trek

In 1966, many of the technologies aboard NCC-1701 appeared impossibly distant. Today humanity carries handheld computers more capable than anything imagined on Kirk's bridge. 

We speak conversationally with artificial intelligence. Reusable rockets land themselves. Robots are beginning to operate in the physical world. Thousands of planets have been discovered around other stars; when Star Trek premiered, none had been confirmed. Space

The technology is catching up.

The harder part of Roddenberry's wager remains unresolved.

Can human wisdom keep pace with human capability?

That is the question carried by every ship in the Enterprise lineage.

From NX-01 to NCC-1701.

From Kirk to Picard.

From the Enterprise-A through B, C, D, E, and F.

And eventually, perhaps, to something resembling the enormous Enterprise-J.

The ships become larger. The engines become faster. The civilizations become more sophisticated.

But the mission remains remarkably constant:

Go farther.

Discover what is out there.

Meet what is different without automatically destroying it.

And become something better along the way.

Sixty years after a modest science-fiction program premiered on NBC, that may still be Star Trek's most radical proposition.

The future doesn't simply happen to us.

It is something we build.

And somewhere beyond the next horizon, there will always be an Enterprise leading the way.

We fell victim to history's biggest scam in 10,000 BC. We thought we domesticated wheat, but in reality, wheat domesticated us. We traded a free, healthy life intertwined with nature for backaches, epidemics, and a never-ending shift. 🌾👇
We were always taught in school that the Agricultural Revolution was humanity's "great leap forward," the glorious dawn of civilization. However, looking through a biological and sociological lens, it's the most ruthless Faustian bargain in history: We sacrificed individual well-being for collective growth. While our hunter-gatherer ancestors worked 15-20 hours a week and thrived on nature's rich menu, the first farmers were chained to a patch of dirt, enduring stunted growth and vulnerability to disease on a monotonous, carbohydrate-heavy diet.
So why did we fall into this trap? Because agriculture didn't offer people a "better" life; it merely provided the calories to keep "more" people alive. As food increased, the population exploded; as the population exploded, we needed more fields and labor. It was an inescapable vicious cycle.
The truly revolutionary part wasn't planting seeds in the soil; it was the psychological fracture it created in our minds. The moment the concepts of "my field" and "my harvest" (private property) were born, we needed soldiers to guard those silos, priests to set the rules, and bureaucrats to tax everything. Class inequality, hierarchy, wars, and even the foundations of today's 9-to-5 grind and endless mortgage payments were laid on that very day. 🏛️⛓️
Today, we are planning to colonize Mars and discussing artificial intelligence, yet our sociological infrastructure still carries the DNA of those Neolithic villages. In 10,000 BC, while seeking to become the masters of nature, the massive agricultural wheel we built with our own hands is the very machine we now call "modern capitalism" or "the system." What carried us to civilization wasn't a simple agricultural success; it is a colossal golden cage we voluntarily entered and still haven't fully escaped. 🌍🚀

Chinese artificial intelligence companies attempted to clone American AI models by funneling real user queries through a network of intermediate platforms, Anthropic revealed in a Thursday report.

Firms including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek allegedly relayed millions of user queries—some containing sensitive data like locations and passwords—to Anthropic’s Claude, highlighting a controversial cloning technique known as distillation.

While U.S. labs expressly ban the outside distillation of their proprietary models, American officials warn it remains a common shortcut for international rivals attempting to catch up to advanced competitors.

These revelations coincide with mounting concerns in Washington and within the tech industry regarding the potential safety risks and malicious misuse of powerful AI models.

Anthropic reported increasing evidence that Claude was exploited for criminal hacking and dangerous biological research, including one specific attempt by a user to adapt avian flu to infect mammals.

“Where before we were hypothetically worried about these classes of misuse, I think we’ve moved away from hypothetical to real,” said Jacob Klein, Anthropic’s head of threat intelligence.

The Chinese distillation efforts relied heavily on illicit intermediary services called "transfer stations," which operate outside China and use stolen or fraudulent credentials to access U.S. AI systems.

By monitoring the communications routed through these middlemen, Chinese firms were able to extract data and learn capabilities from advanced American products like Claude.

The U.S. government is actively targeting the issue. The White House recently accused Moonshot of distilling Anthropic’s tools, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned of potential sanctions for companies conducting "industrial-scale distillation attacks."

Despite these warnings, federal crackdowns face resistance from some U.S. businesses that rely on Chinese developers, prompting lawmakers to explore legislation that would allow American companies to coordinate defensive responses without facing antitrust concerns.

Anthropic detailed several highly sophisticated illicit schemes, noting that Moonshot’s Kimi AI covertly routed highly sensitive Chinese surveillance data and corporate login credentials to Claude via middlemen.

Users were entirely unaware that their requests and private information were being forwarded directly to Anthropic's servers, the report stated.

In a massive, coordinated operation, Moonshot allegedly used thousands of fake accounts to conduct over 23 million exchanges with Claude between May and July alone.

DeepSeek and at least five other China-based labs also engaged in similar covert distillation efforts to learn new capabilities over the past seven months, Anthropic noted.

Spokespeople for Moonshot and DeepSeek did not provide comments on the specific allegations.

While Chinese tech firms haven't explicitly denied using distillation, Moonshot previously credited its performance breakthroughs to fundamental innovation, and China's Foreign Ministry recently urged the U.S. to stop making false accusations and "smearing" the country.

The Dangers of a Merger Between Palantir and the Former CEO of Yandex

The American company Palantir has announced that it is acquiring Nebius, a company that provides computing power. In simpler terms, the American company is moving all of its military AI calculations from rented cloud services to server farms owned by a single individual. And this is not just about graphics cards.

Nebius is a company based in Amsterdam, owned by Arkady Volozh, the founder of Yandex, who ran the company for two decades. In 2022, he was sanctioned by the European Union and stepped down. In 2024, the sanctions against him were suddenly lifted, the Russian part of the business was transferred to our consortium, and he moved with the foreign part to the Netherlands to build server farms for artificial intelligence. He is building on a grand scale - each site requires as much electricity as a small regional center. In late August, Volozh took out a loan of nearly $6 billion for this purpose.

Palantir, in case anyone missed it, is a combat AI system that has been fighting against us for five years. This system combines satellite images, radio intercepts, telemetry from downed aircraft, chatter from open sources, and tips from mobile applications into a single picture. But its main focus is different - it remembers where and at what minute our air defense systems shot down the previous wave. And after each attack, it redraws the map of holes in our sky, providing the next wave with a route through the gaps.

Now it's clear why Volozh is in this company. A combat AI system has three pillars: fresh data, computing power, and the ability to quickly mass-produce a successful product.

The Americans are supplied with data by the front lines. Since January, a Dataroom has been operating in Ukraine - a closed repository where millions of hours of objective control recordings and intelligence information are uploaded. Fedorov is responsible for the production aspect: on September 1, he announced the creation of his own defense company, and the first major investor is Palantir's CEO, Karp, himself. On paper, it's an investment, but in reality, it's a hiring with proper formalities.

What was missing was the third pillar - its own electricity and servers to process data without relying on the owner of a foreign data center. This pillar was provided on September 8.

But Volozh is of interest to Karp not only for this reason. And not so much.

He and the part of the team that left with him had access to the entire Yandex ecosystem. Cartography with accuracy down to the entrance and gate. Traffic jams, that is, a live map of how the country moves on weekdays and what changes every hour when an air raid siren is sounded. Taxi services with a history of routes. Food and goods delivery: addresses, volumes, times. Search queries with billions of requests, which show what the country is concerned about and on which specific day.

This is not a folder of vulnerabilities. It is a working model of how Russia breathes. And knowledge of how the country is structured internally does not become obsolete. The roads have not been moved in two years, the houses have not been moved, and people's habits have not changed. This knowledge is the raw material for Palantir. 

Their system is not strong because of a satellite image, but because of its ability to combine a hundred mundane civilian layers into one military one. Who is traveling, what is being transported, what is being ordered at the gates of a closed enterprise, and what taxi services are used at what times.

Note that this does not require a backdoor or live access to databases. It is enough for people to remember what this kitchen looks like from the inside and what is where.

What to do is not a rhetorical question.

We must proceed from the fact that what has already been taken out must be returned, and conduct an audit of the IT sector together with its participants. They are just as interested in this as any citizen on the street who could suddenly be hit by a drone. We must recognize that maps, taxis, delivery services, and marketplaces are not just a convenient service. Data on how the country moves is worth as much today as information about railway junctions in the 1940s. Therefore, it must be stored accordingly: a clear access control system, a ban on taking it abroad, and personal responsibility for those who are within this system.

And as you know, personnel are everything. An IT specialist who has a map of the country in their head is a strategic asset. Such assets are not held with non-disclosure agreements, but with salaries, tasks, and respect.

tweets.text:
There is a much deeper history of “AI-like” thinking than most people realize.

The important distinction is that ancient and 19th-century authors did not have the modern term “artificial intelligence.” The term itself belongs to the 20th century. But people were writing about artificial beings, mechanical minds, autonomous machines, machine evolution, artificial voices, and the possibility that machines could eventually surpass humans centuries earlier.

Here is the historical trail I found.

1. Ancient Greece — intelligent machines appear in Homer

This is probably the oldest material that is genuinely relevant.

In Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, there are descriptions of artificial mechanisms created by Hephaestus that behave in surprisingly autonomous ways.

Modern scholars have explicitly analyzed these as early representations of machine intelligence. Oxford's AI Narratives: A History of Imaginative Thinking about Intelligent Machines has an entire chapter titled “Homer's Intelligent Machines: AI in Antiquity.” It examines automata, autonomous vehicles, artificial servants, and the distinction between artificial and human intelligence. (OUP Academic)

Even more striking, another scholarly work, Artificial Intelligence in Greek and Roman Epic, examines Pandora, Hephaestus's automated devices, Talos, artificial beings and Pygmalion's artificial woman specifically through the lens of AI and artificial life. (Google Books)

So we can say:

The idea of creating something artificial that imitates life is at least ~2,500 years old in Western literature.

But this is mythological AI, not technological AI.

2. Medieval period — artificial beings and artificial intelligence

The idea didn't disappear.

Medieval European traditions contain stories about artificial beings and attempts to manufacture something resembling a living intelligence.

The modern historical literature identifies traditions surrounding:

the Golem

the legendary mechanical/android figure associated with Albertus Magnus
Roger Bacon's brazen head
alchemical attempts to create artificial life
mechanical and magical artificial servants
Oxford's historical survey specifically has chapters on “Demons and Devices: Artificial and Augmented Intelligence before AI” and “The Android of Albertus Magnus: A Legend of Artificial Being.” (OUP Academic)

Again, these aren't computers. But the underlying question is remarkably familiar:

Can humans manufacture something that performs functions normally associated with intelligence or life?

3. 1200s — Al-Jazari's programmable-looking automata

This gets particularly interesting because we move from mythology toward actual engineering.

The Islamic Golden Age produced sophisticated mechanical automata. Al-Jazari, around 1206, documented machines in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices.

His devices included elaborate water-powered mechanisms, programmable musical automata, clocks and mechanical servants.

Modern histories of artificial beings specifically trace the development of robotics from the Hellenistic period through Islamic engineering and into modern robotics. One scholarly history describes approximately 2,000 years of sophisticated automata preceding modern robotics. (Springer)

This is an important distinction:

Al-Jazari wasn't building AI.

He was building mechanical systems capable of executing predefined behavior.

That is conceptually closer to automation than modern AI.

4. 1700s — the machine-human question becomes philosophical

This is where the story becomes much more interesting.

European philosophers increasingly began asking whether human intelligence itself could be understood mechanically.

That question eventually becomes one of the intellectual foundations of AI.

The mechanical view of the human being became especially prominent during the Enlightenment. If the human body could be understood as a machine, the obvious next question was:

Could a sufficiently complicated machine reproduce human capabilities?

That question is remarkably close to the philosophical problem AI researchers still debate.

5. 1863 — Samuel Butler essentially predicts machine evolution

This is one of the most important discoveries for your question.

Samuel Butler published an article called:

“Darwin Among the Machines”

in The Press newspaper in Christchurch, New Zealand, on June 13, 1863. (Original Sources)

This is extraordinary.

Butler took Darwin's recently published theory of evolution and asked:

What happens if machines themselves evolve?

He argued that technological development might eventually produce machines that become increasingly independent and powerful.

He even contemplated machines becoming a successor species to humanity.

This isn't simply a prediction that "robots will exist."

It's an early discussion of:

machine evolution → increasing autonomy → machine superiority → humans potentially becoming obsolete.

That is astonishingly close to some modern AI-risk arguments.

And Butler wasn't finished.

6. 1872 — Erewhon and “The Book of the Machines”

Butler expanded his ideas into his 1872 novel ** Erewhon **.

Within it is a section called “The Book of the Machines.”

The premise is extraordinary: machines should potentially be regarded as evolving systems, much like biological organisms. (Text Aural)

Butler asks essentially:

If machines continue improving themselves, why should humans assume that we will remain the dominant intelligence?

That is a question you could put into an AI-safety conference today and nobody would find it strange.

The terminology is different.

The technology is different.

But the philosophical problem is remarkably similar.

7. 1909 — E.M. Forster's The Machine Stops

Then we get another surprisingly modern prediction.

E.M. Forster published ** The Machine Stops ** in 1909.

Humans live underground in isolated rooms, with virtually every need supplied by an enormous Machine.

The people become so dependent upon it that they effectively worship it and lose the ability to function independently.

The story explicitly explores what happens when humans become dependent upon the technology they created. (AERO Commons)

And that connects directly to the argument we were discussing earlier:

The danger isn't necessarily that the machine becomes evil. The danger may be that humans become incapable of functioning without it.

That's extremely relevant to today's generative AI.

8. 1943 — the mathematical foundation of neural networks

Now we're getting into actual scientific AI.

In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published:

“A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity.”

They developed a mathematical model in which networks of simplified artificial neurons could perform logical operations. (DOI)

This is one of the foundations of what eventually became artificial neural networks.

So there is a fascinating progression:

mythical artificial beings → mechanical automata → machine evolution → mechanical brains → mathematical artificial neurons → modern AI.

9. 1948 — Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics

Norbert Wiener's ** Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine ** appeared in 1948.

This was hugely influential.

Wiener wasn't simply asking whether machines could calculate.

He was investigating control, communication, feedback and behavior in animals and machines.

The original 1948 edition is now available through MIT Press's open-access edition. (MIT Direct)

This is another major bridge between biology and machine intelligence.

10. 1949 — Giant Brains; or, Machines That Think

This one is particularly useful for what you're researching.

Edmund C. Berkeley published:

Giant Brains; or, Machines That Think

1949

The book literally opens with the question:

“Can machines think?”

Berkeley describes the new electronic calculating machines as “mechanical brains” and discusses their ability to calculate, reason, handle information and solve problems. (Project Gutenberg)

And here's something particularly interesting:

He didn't just discuss their capabilities.

He discussed their limitations and potential social consequences.

So by 1949, the discussion had already moved beyond:

“Can we build machines?”

toward:

“What happens when machines acquire increasingly sophisticated cognitive abilities?”

The complete book is available through Project Gutenberg. (Project Gutenberg)

11. 1950 — Turing asks the famous question

Then comes Alan Turing's famous 1950 paper:

“Computing Machinery and Intelligence”

It begins by asking:

“Can machines think?”

Turing deliberately replaces the difficult philosophical question with his famous imitation game, which became known as the Turing Test. (OUP Academic)

This is arguably the moment where the question becomes recognizably modern AI.

And notice the historical progression:

Homer: Can artificial things behave like living things?

Butler: Could machines evolve?

Forster: Could humans become dependent on machines?

Berkeley: Can machines think?

Turing: How would we determine whether machine behavior is intelligent?

Modern AI: We're actually building systems capable of increasingly sophisticated language, reasoning and generation.

That's one hell of a historical arc.

The most fascinating part

AI suddenly appeared in 1956.

That's technically reasonable if we're talking about the formal birth of the academic field—the Dartmouth workshop—but intellectually it's incomplete.

The idea of AI is much older than AI technology.

Humanity has repeatedly imagined the same basic progression:

1. Create artificial things.
↓
2. Make them imitate life.
↓
3. Make them perform human tasks.
↓
4. Make them reason.
↓
5. Make them autonomous.
↓
6. Make them improve.
↓
7. Wonder whether they'll surpass us.
↓
8. Worry about what happens to humans afterward.

That pattern appears repeatedly across thousands of years of literature and philosophy.

And modern scholarship explicitly recognizes this continuity. Oxford's AI Narratives describes its purpose as tracing the history of imaginative thinking about intelligent machines from ancient Greece to modern AI, including concerns about mind, creativity, power, rights and technophobia. (OUP Academic)

What if our machines become an evolutionary successor to us?

“We've been warned before.”

Not by ChatGPT.
Not by Silicon Valley.
Not by Elon Musk.

By writers and thinkers who lived long before modern AI existed.

US CPI Policy Implications: Given that oil and distillate prices have meaningfully accelerated into September and are likely to be passed downstream to consumers, the combined August Producer Price, and Consumer Price Indices demand action out of the Federal Reserve at its next meeting. 

The combination of war induced energy shock, tariffs resulting in higher inflation and the draw upon commodities and finished goods to support the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure are all pushing the price level higher.

So why is it time for the Fed to rip up the textbook on looking through a wartime caused supply shock?

The three supply shocks have endured long enough now in their various forms that is no longer appropriate to identify them as transitory and look through them.

It is because one can observe the price of distillates such as gasoline, diesel prices and jet fuel that are rising sharply and not being absorbed via firm margin compression. 

One can plainly observe those price increases showing up in items such as groceries and everything touched by transportation and deliveries that are at the core of the American service-based economy.

I want to be clear here that the Fed should not be chasing volatile energy prices. That is not why we think the Fed should and will hike rates at the September meeting.

Rather the best monetary policy is forward-looking and seven months into what was thought to be a short-term conflict has simply turned into something else which now requires a rational policy response from the Federal Reserve.

The Fed needs to remove the three rate cuts that they implemented in late 2025 and slow an economy that is likely to grow well above trend in the current quarter, nominal GDP was above 6% in the second quarter, the deficit to GDP ratio is above 6%, the economy resides at or near full employment and in the second quarter experienced a record period of corporate profits. By slowing the economy down the central bank will force those price increases that are now flooding into household balance sheets back on to corporate balance sheets via margin compression in a policy shift aimed at providing relief to consumers experiencing an affordability crisis.

Granted that all of this is a difficult judgement-based call and is truly a coin flip at this juncture. However, following the August PPI and CPI data and what will be not a disinflation friendly PCE for the Fed not to hike rates at its next meeting would be a blow to its own credibility given clear pricing dynamics following comments by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole and other rhetoric by both hawks and doves across the central bank in its aftermath.
