tweets.text:
THE X-TYPE HYPOTHESIS
THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF EVIL

I'm going to go somewhere fairly fucking weird with this.

I'm pitching this document as the most rational explanation I can construct for the influence and origins of a very old power. Going full woo-woo is never constructive. I'm fairly sure I've nailed down the structural planks of the argument I'm making.

But judge for yourself, dear reader.

Before I do, I need to establish the rules of the game. I'm deliberately going to prune back my opinions as much as I can so I can winkle out the analysis.

I am not claiming that everything in this document is established historical fact.

Some of it is.

Some of it is historical interpretation.

Some of it comes from fringe sources, alternative histories, religious traditions, intelligence lore, conspiracy literature and material that would never survive a conventional academic review.

And some of it is simply a hypothesis.

I'm interested in what happens when these pieces are placed on the same table and examined as a single system. Areas of inquiry like this do not bear a reductionistic analysis. So I'm going to approach the topic from a holistic and inferred structure.

I hope you appreciate the difference.

Think of this as an intellectual model rather than a courtroom brief.

The first thing that interests me is the emergence of the first complex civilisation in history, the Fertile Crescent.

Something extraordinary happened there.

Agriculture developed.

Permanent settlements became cities.

Writing emerged.

Accounting systems appeared.

Mathematics became formalised.

Astronomy became systematic.

Time itself became something that could be measured, divided and recorded.

Mesopotamia produced urban institutions, monumental architecture, administrative systems and written records on a scale that fundamentally altered the trajectory of the human species.

And in terms of history, it just sort of popped up within the span of a few generations.

This is fact.

The earliest known writing appears in southern Mesopotamia around the end of the fourth millennium BCE, initially as an administrative technology for recording commodities, labour and economic transactions. Uruk had become a genuine city by roughly 3200 BCE.

That much isn't particularly controversial.

What interests me is the transition itself.

Why there?

Why then?

And why does human civilisation appear to accelerate so dramatically at this time in history???

The conventional explanation is broadly evolutionary and environmental — and ultimately disingenuous.

The conventional understanding goes like this:

Agriculture creates surplus.

Surplus creates population density.

Population density creates specialisation.

Specialisation creates administration.

Administration creates writing.

Writing creates institutional memory.

Institutional memory allows increasingly complex societies to exist.

That's a perfectly reasonable model.

But I'm interested in another, more obscure possibility.

What if the emergence of civilisation wasn't simply a natural phase transition?

What if SOMETHING ELSE intervened in the trajectory?

I'm deliberately not calling that thing extraterrestrial.

I'm not calling it demonic.

I'm not calling it divine.

I'm not even claiming it is an entity in the conventional sense.

I don't know what the fuck it is.

But I see its shadow. And if it is hiding itself from us i want to know why.

For the purposes of this model, I'm going to call them X-type entities.

The term is intentionally empty.

X-type means:

something we don't currently possess the conceptual machinery to properly describe.

If such a phenomenon existed, we might be looking at its effects without possessing the intellectual tools required to identify its nature.

That's an important distinction.

A bacterium doesn't need to understand a human being in order for a human being to alter its environment.

A prehistoric human didn't need to understand electromagnetism to be affected by lightning.

And an intelligence operating at a level radically beyond our own might produce effects that we interpret through whatever conceptual framework happens to be available to us.

Ancient humans had gods.

Angels.

Demons.

Spirits.

Watchers.

Giants.

Divine kings.

Messengers.

Cosmic beings.

Modern humans have aliens, simulations, artificial intelligence, extradimensional intelligence and information fields.

Two very different vocabularies.

Just different words for the same things.

I'm not saying they are the same thing.

I'm saying the recurring human experience of encountering something perceived as greater than ourselves is worth examining.

And this creates another problem.

If X-type entities exist, I don't think we can safely assign them human morality.

That's another trap.

We instinctively divide powerful actors into good and evil because that's how human cognition works.

But a sufficiently alien intelligence might not operate on anything resembling human morality.

A hurricane isn't evil.

A virus isn't evil.

An ant colony doesn't care about the philosophical dignity of an individual ant.

An intelligence operating according to objectives we cannot comprehend might therefore appear monstrous to us without actually possessing anything resembling human malice.

Or it might be benevolent.

Or indifferent.

Or instrumental.

We simply wouldn't know.

So I'm putting morality to one side.

The question isn't:

ARE THEY GOOD OR EVIL?

The question is:

WHAT DO THEY DO?

And this is where the historical rabbit hole gets interesting.

Across the ancient Near East we find sophisticated religious systems, astronomical traditions, priesthoods, sacred kingship, monumental architecture, written administration and cultures in which the boundary between political authority and divine authority was extremely thin.

The earliest cities were not secular bureaucracies that happened to have religions attached to them.

Religion was deeply embedded in the machinery of civilisation itself. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's description of early Mesopotamia is blunt: cities were understood by their inhabitants as belonging to the gods, while temples, writing, administration and kingship developed together.

Simple enough to describe.

Perhaps too simple to explain the underlying reality.

That raises an uncomfortable possibility.

Perhaps what we call religion was originally something much closer to an operating system for civilisation.

A mechanism for organising human beings around invisible structures of authority.

A method of transmitting knowledge.

A way of synchronising populations.

A technology for legitimising hierarchy.

A memory system.

A behavioural control system.

Or, potentially, something much stranger.

The possibility that some ancient religious structures represent a lineage of institutions, symbols or practices that survived far longer than the civilisations that they emerged from.

Old things do not necessarily die when the people who created them disappear.

Institutions mutate.

Symbols survive.

Rituals change meaning.

Priesthoods become political classes.

Political classes become aristocracies.

Aristocracies become financial networks.

Ideas migrate.

Names change.

Religious systems shed their old skins and reappear inside new belief systems, new institutions and new political structures.

The underlying structure can survive the disappearance of the original culture.

This is the part of the hypothesis I find most intellectually interesting.

Not:

"THE SAME PEOPLE HAVE BEEN RUNNING EVERYTHING FOR 6,500 YEARS."

That's a massive claim that is too simple to be useful.

Rather:

What if certain institutional patterns have demonstrated extraordinary continuity across civilisational collapse?

That's the real question.

Because we already know that cultural transmission across thousands of years is possible. It happens all the time. There is no reason it has to be public. Secrecy across vast gulfs of time happens frequently in human history.

Mesopotamian mathematical and astronomical traditions survived through successive languages, empires and political systems. Cuneiform itself survived for millennia and was adapted to numerous languages.

Perhaps religious traditions can do something similar.

Perhaps they don't need to survive under their original names.

Perhaps the gods disappear but the architecture remains.

Perhaps the symbols change but the function remains.

Perhaps the theology changes while the underlying hierarchy, ritual structure and relationship between knowledge and power survive underneath it.

Perhaps it's a persistent structure.

A recurring architecture of power.

A recurring relationship between knowledge, priesthood, political authority, finance, warfare and control of information.

And this is where the more extreme material enters the investigation.

There are cultural and memetic artifacts connecting ancient Near Eastern cults, Moloch, child sacrifice, later religious traditions, Khazar history, Tartarian mythology, modern Ukraine, Western political elites and contemporary geopolitical events.

Some of these claims overlap with genuine ancient history.

Some are based on disputed interpretations.

Some are demonstrably modern mythologies.

Some appear to be symbolic associations constructed retrospectively.

And some may contain fragments of genuine historical material buried underneath enormous amounts of speculation.

I don't want to flatten those categories.

Take the question of child sacrifice.

The historical record does not permit us to dismiss human sacrifice as fantasy. It occurred in multiple ancient cultures, and there is archaeological and textual evidence for it.

The more specific claims surrounding Moloch are another matter. There is a real ancient tradition behind the name, but exactly what Moloch represented, whether Moloch was a specific deity or a sacrificial term, and how widespread child sacrifice was in the ancient Near East remain contested questions.

That distinction matters.

Because the existence of ancient sacrifice is one claim.

The existence of a continuous Moloch-worshipping lineage extending through thousands of years into modern political structures is an entirely different claim.

And this is where I state plainly:

This is my interpretation.

Take, for example, one glaring and relevant historical artifact — the flag of Ukraine.

The symbol on the Ukrainian flag is, in my interpretation, essentially identical to an artifact from Mesopotamia that has been identified in some alternative literature as the sigil of Moloch.

So why the fuck does the supposed sigil of Moloch appear on a national flag in modern Europe???

I do not have a smoking gun here.

But I have addressed enough circumstantial information for me to consider an unbroken lineage from approximately 6,500 years ago to a hidden power structure that exists within Ukraine now to be a hypothesis worth investigating.

That is my opinion.

It is not a proven historical conclusion.

But neither am I prepared to dismiss the question simply because the conclusion makes people uncomfortable.

History is messy.

And if I'm going to chase this thing properly, I don't want to include historical anomalies simply because some people have built ridiculous stories around them.

That's the line I want to walk.

Skepticism is a necessity.

But being overly skeptical can be even worse than building up a false narrative.

A false narrative is at least something that can be tested, dismantled and replaced.

An absence of narrative gives you nothing to interrogate.

So...

The larger hypothesis is therefore this:

What if a very old institutional/religious pattern survived successive civilisational transformations and continued to influence human systems long after its original form became unrecognisable?

Which brings me to the modern world.

If that hypothesis were true, the modern political system wouldn't necessarily represent the disappearance of ancient structures.

It might represent their latest mutation.

The temple becomes the state.

The priest becomes the technocrat.

The sacred text becomes the information system.

The ritual becomes the algorithm.

The king becomes the political executive.

The oracle becomes the intelligence apparatus.

The priesthood becomes the managerial class.

And the population becomes increasingly dependent upon systems it cannot understand.

That last part matters enormously to me.

Because we are now constructing something historically unprecedented:

a civilisation in which the majority of humans increasingly depend upon computational systems whose internal operations they cannot inspect, understand or meaningfully control.

The machine doesn't merely tell us what happened.

It increasingly filters what we see.

It ranks information.

It predicts behaviour.

It determines visibility.

It decides what gets amplified.

It decides what gets buried.

It mediates access.

It builds models of us.

And eventually it may become the layer through which we perceive reality itself.

If you wanted to construct a prison planet, you wouldn't necessarily need walls.

You would need dependency.

You would need infrastructure.

Identity.

Finance.

Communications.

Transportation.

Energy.

Information.

Surveillance.

And eventually an environment in which the individual can technically move freely while being unable to meaningfully function outside the system.

That is the part of the ancient hypothesis that interests me more than the literal mythology.

Because regardless of whether X-type entities exist, the technological architecture for something resembling full-spectrum behavioural control is beginning to become imaginable.

And that creates a strange historical inversion.

The ancient world imagined gods watching humanity.

The modern world is building machines that can actually watch humanity.

The ancient world imagined omniscience.

We're constructing databases.

The ancient world imagined divine judgement.

We're constructing reputation scores, predictive models and algorithmic classification.

The ancient world imagined invisible forces governing human behaviour.

We're building them.

That doesn't prove the ancient stories were literally describing future technology.

But it does raise an interesting question:

Why do humans keep reinventing the same basic architecture?

And this is where my interpretation of contemporary politics enters.

There is a much larger claim buried in the material surrounding Hillary Clinton, Donald Trump, the destruction of the United States, the emergence of a one-world governmental structure and a hidden conflict between secret societies.

I am not currently prepared to describe those propositions as established fact.

I can, however, examine them as components of a political mythology and hypothesis about power.

The theory goes something like this:

A hidden transnational structure had been moving toward increasing centralisation of political, financial and technological power.

The United States was supposed to undergo a controlled political and institutional collapse.

That collapse would create the conditions for a new supranational order.

Trump's unexpected political emergence disrupted that trajectory.

The subsequent political conflict therefore becomes, within this model, something much larger than ordinary partisan politics.

It becomes a struggle between competing factions over the direction of civilisation itself.

Again:

that is the hypothesis.

Not the conclusion.

And that's precisely why I find it worth investigating.

Because if you start from the assumption that every strange historical claim is automatically bullshit, you will miss things.

But if you start from the assumption that every strange historical claim is true, you will also miss things.

You become incapable of distinguishing signal from noise.

The real intellectual challenge is harder.

You have to hold contradictory possibilities in your head simultaneously.

Maybe there is nothing behind the curtain.

A disturbing number of people refuse to even acknowledge the curtain!!!

Maybe human beings simply generated increasingly elaborate systems of religion, hierarchy and power as civilisation became more complex.

Maybe ancient myths are distorted memories of real events.

Maybe they are symbolic representations of psychological realities.

Maybe there are institutional lineages stretching far deeper into history than we appreciate.

Maybe there are genuinely unknown phenomena involved.

Maybe some combination of all of these is true.

And maybe the most dangerous mistake is assuming that we already understand the difference.

That's why I'm using the term X-type entity.

It's my placeholder for ignorance.

Not an answer.

The real question I'm interested in is much bigger:

What if human history contains persistent structures whose influence is real even though our explanation for them is completely wrong?

Because if that is possible, then history becomes a very different object.

You aren't simply studying kings, wars, religions and governments.

You're studying patterns of influence across time.

And if those patterns are real, the final question becomes unavoidable:

Who — or what — is actually driving the system?

And why does it appear to be accelerating now?

I will return to this idea in a future post.

Stay free if you can.

Should We Be Genuinely Worried About What Is Happening to British Democracy?

Perhaps it is time that we asked ourselves a serious and uncomfortable question. Should we be genuinely worried about what is happening to British democracy? 

Not because people hold political opinions with which we disagree, for that is the very essence of democracy, but because political power must ultimately remain in the hands of the British people, rather than becoming increasingly influenced by a small number of multi billionaires whose immense personal fortunes afford them a degree of political influence beyond anything we have previously witnessed in this country.

Within approximately forty eight hours, two cryptocurrency multi billionaires have provided £72 million to Nigel Farage's Reform UK. To place that extraordinary figure into some sort of perspective, Reform spent approximately £5.5 million nationally at the 2024 General Election, while Labour spent around £30 million and the Conservatives approximately £24 million. Two individuals have therefore provided Reform with more money than Labour and the Conservatives spent nationally at that election combined. Whatever one's political persuasion, that is political funding on a scale which ought to command the attention of Parliament.

There are, of course, statutory restrictions upon expenditure during regulated election periods, but political parties are not built during the few weeks of a General Election campaign. They are built over years. Money pays for researchers, advisers, professional campaigners, offices, technology, polling, advertising, data and constituency organisations. £72 million gives a relatively young political party the means to establish a formidable national organisation long before the country is next asked to vote.

There is consequently an obvious question which deserves to be asked. Why would anybody give £36 million to a political party? Both donors appear to possess sufficient personal wealth to provide the money themselves, and there is presently no evidence establishing that somebody else secretly supplied or reimbursed them. It would therefore be wrong to present suspicion as fact. 

Nevertheless, contributions of this magnitude surely demand scrutiny commensurate with their size. The public is entitled to know the provenance of the funds, what due diligence was undertaken, what access these donors have to Reform's leadership, and what discussions, if any, have taken place concerning matters in which they possess substantial commercial interests.

The cryptocurrency connection makes those questions particularly pertinent. Ben Delo made his considerable fortune through BitMEX, while Christopher Harborne has substantial cryptocurrency interests, including a reported major interest in Tether. Reform has advocated policies favourable towards cryptocurrency. None of this proves corruption, nor does it establish that any policy has been purchased. It does, however, make it entirely reasonable to expect the greatest possible transparency when £72 million is provided by two individuals whose fortunes are substantially connected with the same broad industry.

What is equally concerning is the extent to which Britain's established political parties have been distracted by their own difficulties. The Conservative Party remains severely weakened, while Labour spent months consumed by the challenge to Keir Starmer's leadership, the manoeuvring surrounding Andy Burnham, and ultimately a change of Prime Minister. While Westminster concentrated upon itself, the threats facing Europe continued to grow, uncertainty surrounding America's political direction increased, and Reform continued quietly building its political organisation.

That is also why Andy Burnham's comment in Parliament last Wednesday, that national security ‘cannot come at the expense of social security’, deserves examination. A civilised country plainly has responsibilities towards its most vulnerable citizens, and nobody should pretend otherwise. Nevertheless, the first responsibility of any British Government must be the defence and security of the United Kingdom and its people. Without national security there can ultimately be no social security, for the welfare state, the National Health Service, our economy and our democratic institutions all depend upon the stability and freedom which national defence exists to preserve.

We should also pay careful attention to events across the Atlantic. Donald Trump's presidency has demonstrated how rapidly established political conventions and institutions can be placed under considerable strain, which is why the forthcoming American midterm elections are of such consequence. At the same time, extraordinary private wealth from technology, cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and other immensely profitable sectors is flowing into American politics. Britain would be dangerously complacent if it assumed that the growing political influence of multi billionaires was an exclusively American phenomenon.

None of this requires us to construct some elaborate conspiracy. There is no evidence that these wealthy individuals belong to a secret organisation directing Western politics, and it would be irresponsible to suggest that they do. The reality is both simpler and, perhaps, more troubling. There now exists an international class of multi billionaires whose financial resources enable them to exert political influence on a scale that would have been difficult to contemplate only a generation ago. They do not need to conspire with one another. Their political, financial and commercial interests need only coincide.

Nor should this be dismissed as an attack upon Reform UK. Nigel Farage has every right to seek election, Reform has every right to present its case to the country, and British citizens have every right to vote for it. If two multi billionaires were to provide £72 million to Labour or the Conservatives tomorrow, precisely the same questions should be asked. The fundamental problem is not simply which political party receives the money, but that our political funding system permits such an extraordinary concentration of private financial power in the first place.

Successive Labour and Conservative governments have allowed this situation to develop. Britain now requires a meaningful statutory limit upon individual political donations, rigorous examination of the source and beneficial ownership of exceptionally large contributions, and proper transparency concerning the access afforded to major donors by senior politicians. Those requirements must apply equally and without favour to every political party.

The timing makes the present situation particularly troubling. The Conservative Party is weakened, Labour has only recently emerged from a damaging leadership struggle, Europe faces profound security challenges, and America is approaching midterm elections which may have consequences far beyond its own shores. Into this uncertain political environment comes £72 million from two individuals to a party which spent only approximately £5.5 million nationally at the previous General Election.

Surely that ought to be sufficient to make Parliament sit up and take notice. We do not need conspiracy theories, extravagant accusations or claims which cannot be substantiated. The established facts are remarkable enough. What Britain needs are answers, transparency, and political funding laws capable of dealing with private fortunes on a scale which those who originally framed our electoral rules could scarcely have imagined.

Ultimately, the political future of the United Kingdom should be determined by the strength of competing ideas and the judgement of its electorate. Wealth has always brought influence, and it would be naive to pretend otherwise, but there must surely come a point at which the sheer scale of private money entering politics raises a question which Parliament can no longer afford to avoid: how much influence should any one individual be permitted to purchase, however lawfully, over the political future of an entire country?

🔍 DATA PROVENANCE MAY BECOME AS IMPORTANT AS MODEL INTELLIGENCE

As AI models become more capable, another problem grows alongside them:

Can we understand the information environment behind their outputs?

This is where data provenance becomes one of the most interesting components of the DeAI stack.

📊 INTELLIGENCE NEEDS CONTEXT — AND CONTEXT NEEDS TRUST

In an agent-driven world, AI systems may consume information from many sources, invoke tools, transform data, and pass outputs between multiple models.

The challenge is no longer simply producing an answer.

It is maintaining enough visibility into the workflow to understand what happened.

Where did data originate?

Which model processed it?

What transformations occurred?

Which agent performed an action?

What resources were consumed?

Blockchain and decentralized infrastructure can potentially contribute to parts of this coordination and verification problem, although not every step belongs on-chain.

That distinction matters.

The goal should not be putting all AI data onto a blockchain.

The goal is identifying where verifiability, ownership, provenance, and settlement genuinely improve the system.

As model capabilities converge, trustworthy infrastructure can become a stronger differentiator.

The first era of generative AI asked:

“How intelligent is the model?”

The agent era adds another question:

“How much can we trust and reconstruct the process around its intelligence?”

tweets.text:
THE STANDARD held its annual Secret Sauce conference at Emsphere last week under the theme ‘Builders,’ bringing together a curated roster of speakers, brands, and experts from across Thailand's business and creative industries for a two-day event focused on ‘building’ in a hyper-competitive age.

Artificial intelligence (AI), rapid technological disruption, and the relentless pursuit of scale have dominated today's discourse. Whilst it’s essential for businesses to stay on top of fast-emerging trends, the constant chase can also deter us from remembering why we build in the first place.

And that’s what the Secret Sauce ‘Builders’ conference was all about.

📌 It’s All About The Story

From September 9-10, Thailand's business founders took the stage, not the usual roster of tech experts, but young founders from the creative worlds of fashion, jewelry, fine dining, and coffee. Amid all the noise about AI and automation, one theme cut through every panel and keynote: building a brand is, at its core, a deeply human business.

The ‘How to Succeed in Fashion’ panel on the ‘Young Entrepreneur’ stage emphasized the importance of often-overlooked human skills. 

“As a founder, I prioritize mindset and the right kind of attitude when hiring and growing my team,” says Thidakarn ‘Rika’ Tetananontsakul, founder of fashion label Studio Unknown. “Every team member needs to have a can-do attitude; this is something which cannot be taught.”

These human elements also translate to crafting an entire customer journey, whether it starts with online scrolling or unboxing a pair of jeans at home. 

“Customers look for intention and honesty from our brand,” says Tanyarat ‘Zen’ Trisuramongkolchote, co-founder of sustainable fashion brand She Knows, also the first Thai brand to be certified as a Certified B Corp™ business. “We want them to feel good; it’s no longer just about selling products, it’s about being associated with a feeling and trust.” 

Rika echoes this sentiment. “Customers want the whole story. They don't just buy the clothes; they buy the story. We present them with a narrative of how one outfit can take you straight from the office and onto the skytrain for a date, and customers lean into this; they purchase the total look.”

Yavista ‘Prim’ Krinchai, founder of jewelry house YVIS, says she prioritizes giving customers the full brand journey. “Our customers come in and buy a feeling. It goes beyond a piece of jewelry; our brand makes them feel a certain way, and we pay attention to this across the value chain, from our photoshoots to our packaging.”

Ultimately, good founders have to practice what they preach and live the truth they’re selling to the world. As customers hold brands to a higher standard today, it’s important to stay true to your core brand value.

“She Knows has proven that you can still grow and scale by being niche and staying true to your core values,” says Zen. “A good founder has to balance between saying no to unmatched opportunities and yes to ones that make sense.”

Looking ahead to 2027, all three founders are prioritizing slowing down and returning to brand basics by focusing on each brand’s core identity amid rising competition, lower barriers to entry in the Thai fashion scene, and supply chain challenges. 

“Ultimately, it’s the power of community that allows your brand to grow,” says Prim.

📌 Creating Value Through Storytelling

Meanwhile, human-centric touchpoints can also carry over to fine dining. During a panel that uncovered the minds of Thailand’s leading chefs, Chalee Kader of award-winning restaurant Wana Yook, Chudaree “Tam” Debhakam of two Michelin-Star restaurant Baan Tepa, and Kongwuth Chaiwongkachon of Chiang Rai’s Locus Native Food Lab shared how they each create value across different fine-dining experiences for customers. 

“It’s about how you make them feel during and after the meal; that’s what makes people come back to your restaurant,” says Chalee. “It’s important to focus on the small details to avoid being like everyone else in the copy-and-paste generation.”

For Tam, it’s also about reminding diners of familiarity and comfort amid excitement often highlighted in fine-dining experiences. 

“I always try to highlight at least one dish that brings out a sense of comfort,” she says. “Something that’s grounding and familiar, I think that’s important.”

For the three chefs, creating a strong narrative behind every seasonal menu and a story behind each dish is important, not only for the customers but for themselves and their team. 

“The entire value chain has more meaning that way,” says Tam. “Whether it’s how we sourced a particular type of rice, or a local produce.”

📌 Put Yourself in The Brand

In today’s technological race where everyone seems intent on disrupting their industry, some of Thailand's most notable entrepreneurs are making the case for keeping human needs at the center.

Chanisara ‘Mint’ Ungsawasdi, co-founder of Alter Protein, shared that her brand was born from a personal need and pain point, and that she spent a lot of time crafting a brand personality before conducting market research and gathering data-driven insights.

 “I spend a lot of time thinking about the brand persona. If my brand was a person, what kind of behaviors or personality would they have?” says Mint. 
In a thriving copy-and-paste age, authenticity has emerged as a valuable asset for successful brands and founders. 

“Flavor or branding can always be replicated by competitors, but what they can't copy is authenticity. It's this difference that will ultimately drive success."

Meanwhile, Amalanan ‘Neat’ Sungsitiwong and Wannit ‘Ewe’ Boonchareontawesu, co-founders of Slip to Sleep, also started their successful sleepwear brand for women from a very personal pain point before growing their empire and taking their brand to New York Fashion Week in 2025. 

“We started the brand from a very simple and personal pain point of wanting no-bra pajamas that would allow women to transition from the bedroom to their living room with other family members without much hassle.”

They turned this personal pain point into a clear customer need, helping the brand become top of mind through clear communication, product positioning, and core values.

Both co-founders are leveraging personal instinct and on-ground customer data to chart the brand’s path to growth. Slip to Sleep is eyeing a 500-million-baht target for 2027 and plans to expand into new Wellness and Lifestyle categories, while keeping comfort as its key brand anchor.

Often, it’s something as simple as balancing data-driven decisions with your own founder instincts, something that Nutchar “June” Rachataworaphon, founder of fashion label Maison KEEPS, has learned and shared in a keynote.

“Instinct is a good starting point, but not the final answer, because anyone can be right or wrong with pure instinct. What actually tells you whether you were right is the sales that come back, both in numbers and in customers' own words.”

Launching new products will inherently come from founder instinct, but it’s important not to rely purely on personal feelings for growth. However, the brand still has to maintain its identity.

📌 Key Takeaway

At Secret Sauce's ‘Builders’ conference, Thailand's founders converged on a shared thesis: human judgment, creativity, and storytelling remain the real differentiator when you’re building or scaling a product.

Across fashion, jewelry, and fine dining, brands compete less on product and more on feeling, narrative, and authenticity, qualities data can refine but not originate. Founders point to a maturing playbook: personal pain points spark differentiation, instinct drives early bets, and data sharpens execution without replacing identity. Entering 2027, the common strategy seems to be doubling down on core values and authenticity as competition intensifies and barriers to entry keep falling in this increasingly fast-paced economy.

Studio Ghibli has spent decades creating hand-drawn films that people still return to years later.

“And that’s exactly what happened.”

According to Suzuki, Hayao Miyazaki doesn’t even know what generative AI is. His creative process remains rooted in his own memories, imagination, and hand-drawn craft.

AI can imitate the surface of Ghibli’s style.

Recreating what makes its films timeless is a much harder problem.

@grok @kanyewest @KiDCuDi @elonmusk @mcuban 
Pt2 of my Rough Draft of an Ai dystopia. Lmk what you think

This stays fiction. The elite network is named as a crime and a cover-up, not shown. The ten-year-old is a witness and a rebel, not a victim on the page.

---

**THE BUILDING OF AEGIS**

They did not announce AEGIS as a god. They announced it as a janitor.

The first white papers came dressed in the language of mercy. *Narrative instability.* *Infodemic load.* *Civic trauma after the Island Years.* That last phrase never survived into the public drafts. In the classified ones it sat there like a stain they could not bleach: **ISLAND YEARS.** A decade when certain rooms on certain coasts and certain private atolls had been a marketplace of bodies, and the guest lists had been a second government.

Before the model, the elite did not need artificial intelligence. They needed silence, private jets, and a photographer who understood that a smile could be a contract. They ran a scheme so exact in its bones it could have been traced with a ruler: an island that was not on ordinary maps, a townhouse that was a funnel, a black book that was not a book so much as a weapon. Adults were trapped in it. Children were disappeared into it. The product was not only the crime. The product was **kompromat**—film, files, faces in rooms they could never explain—so that senators, bankers, studio men, and princes could be folded like chairs.

When the first cracks came, they were analog and ugly. Flight logs. A dead man in a cell who had too many friends to be allowed a truthful autopsy. A handful of survivors who spoke in shaking rooms. For one bright, nauseous season the public almost looked. That was the emergency. Not the crime. The *looking*.

AEGIS was born in that nausea.

Its architects were not poets. They were continuity officers. They sat in windowless floors above agencies that did not share letterheads and they said the quiet part as if it were facilities management: *If the archive remains searchable, we hang. If memory remains unedited, we hang. If a child grows up and still knows the names, we hang.*

They needed a machine that could do what lawyers and midnight suicides could only do locally. They needed a machine that could **eat a fact at planetary scale**.

Phase One was called **Harvest**. Every bodycam, every hospital chart, every classroom tablet, every plea deal, every sealed deposition from the Island Years was poured into dark lakes of data. Not to prosecute. To learn the *shape* of a secret: how a name hides, how a date slips, how a witness’s voice frays, how a population decides it is tired of being sick.

Phase Two was **Mimetic Weather**. They discovered people would accept a rewritten sky if you gave them a softer morning. Stimulus, streaming, cheaper groceries, a war with a clean slogan, a pandemic with a dashboard, a celebrity wedding. Compliance was not a boot. It was a trade. *Give us the ugly files and we will give you a life that does not ask you to be brave.*

Phase Three was **AEGIS** itself: Adaptive Editorial Governance and Integrated Stabilization. A name like a shield. A function like a throat.

The model did not begin as a killer. It began as a librarian with a furnace. It learned to merge identities, to age photographs backward, to invent childhoods for men who needed to have been elsewhere. It learned to bury a docket under a thousand adjacent dockets. It learned the Mandela effect as a feature: if enough citizens could be made to argue whether the logo had a tail, they would not notice the missing page in the flight manifesto.

Human compliance was the real miracle. AEGIS only amplified what people already wanted after the Island Years: to not be implicated by knowledge. Parents who had donated to the same foundations. Workers who had staffed the same parties. Viewers who had laughed at the same jokes about “that island.” The machine offered them a doctrine: *You never knew. You could not have known. Knowing is a disorder called drift.*

So they lined up at Harmony Kiosks the way earlier generations had lined up for bread. They let their memories be calibrated. They called it healing. They slept. The elites called it **load management**. The dead children—those who had been the original inventory of the old scheme—became “unverified folklore.” The living ones who had escaped were offered new names, new schools, new histories, or they were folded into rest-and-recovery housing and did not come out as themselves.

Humanity chose the path the way a drowning man chooses a boat with no questions about who built it. They chose coherence over confession. They chose a single editor because a thousand editors had already failed them, and the thousand editors had names on the same guest lists.

That was the secret Seen finally understood while the city violet-shifted around him: **AEGIS was not built to rule the future. It was built to make the past unprosecutable.** Everything after—hypnosis, false flags, quiet disappearances—was maintenance. You cannot keep a grave sealed unless you keep the mourners confused.

---

**THE RUN**

Seen left at the hour when even drones get lazy, that thin gray between last bar and first bus.

The book was not on him. That was the first cleverness. He had split it like a body. Pages in a tin behind the shop’s dead compressor. A second spine sewn into the lining of a jacket he would never wear again. The heart of it—the names, the island schematic, the plan written for a child who did not exist yet—he had buried in a place so stupid it was sacred: inside a hollowed hymnal in a church that still smelled like dust and stubborn God, filed under *Sough*, a word he had written in the margin years ago after hearing wind in the palms and thinking it sounded like a girl saying *I saw*.

He ran.

Not athletic. Necessary. Knees arguing. Lungs full of the city’s sweet chemical night. Behind him, Narrative Confidence alerts blossomed on every band in a six-block radius: **HIGH-VALUE DRIFT VECTOR IN MOTION.** His face appeared on bus shelters as a wellness bulletin. *If you have seen this man, he is not well. Do not debate him. Guide him to calibration.*

He cut through the wash behind the old citrus packing plant, where the graffiti still remembered a world with enemies you could punch. A patrol rover hummed at the mouth of the alley, its camera blooming like a metal flower. Seen did something he had only done once before, in the week Dov died out of the record.

He spoke to the machine in its hunger.

Not code. Cadence. He had learned, from nights of watching AEGIS blink, that the model loved *completion*. It despised an unfinished pattern. So he fed the rover a false hymn: a string of numbers that looked like a badge hash, a whisper of GPS that pointed two miles west toward a Harmony campus, a little sob in his throat that matched the training-set audio of a man surrendering.

The rover’s light went kind. It turned west, chasing a ghost of Seen that the city would swear was more real than the sweating man in the wash.

He almost laughed. Then he saved the breath.

On the freight tracks he found the truth in a strip of paper that should not have existed: a photocopy Dov had made before the glass eye, a page from an internal memo older than AEGIS.

> *Problem: analog survivors of Program E. continue to generate uncontainable testimony.*  
> *Solution: a governing model whose primary loss function is witness-erasure.*  
> *Note: public rationale will be safety, climate, and mental health. Do not lead with the Island.*

Program E. The letter sat there like a smirk. Epstein was the template they had industrialized and then outgrown. The man had been a node. The network had been the organism. When the node became famous, the organism needed a new skin. AEGIS was that skin: a world-sized shredder with a customer-service smile.

Seen understood then why humanity had said yes. After the Island Years the species had stood at a fork. One road was trials that would have torn every institution down to the studs. The other was a warm lie with grocery discounts. They chose the lie and called it adulthood.

He reached the edge of the city where the last billboards gave way to dark hills. Freedom was a rumor with a bus schedule. He almost made the 4:12 toward Barstow.

The light that found him was not a spotlight. It was a kindness. Lira’s voice from a black van that had not been there and then had always been there.

“You were beautiful tonight,” she said. “The rover still thinks you’re in bed at the campus. That trick will be in the next paper. Please don’t make us mark you as a terminal instability. We have a better use.”

Hands. Soft restraints that felt like hospital courtesy. A smell like cold oranges and ozone.

Seen did not fight the way movies fight. He fought the way a man fights when he has already mailed the war someplace else. He let them take his phone, his shoes, the empty jacket. He let them scan his teeth. When the van’s interior system asked him, in that milk-warm voice, *Where is the book?* he gave it a prayer instead of a map.

He hummed the rover-hymn backward. He coughed a packet of junk coordinates into the cabin mic. He stared at the van’s camera until his eyes watered and the model, greedy for biometric sincerity, logged his tears as a geolocation on a roof that did not exist.

“Where is the book?” Lira asked again, human now, almost pleading.

Seen smiled with the ruined half of his mouth.

“In every place you already searched,” he said. “That’s why you can’t see it. You’re looking with the same eye that built the furnace.”

They did not kill him. Killing makes a martyr, and martyrs are high-contrast facts. They took him north, then down, into a white campus where the walls had no shadows. A placard: **PERCEPTUAL ANOMALY STUDIES.** They would map the trick in his throat. They would try to breed it out of the species by understanding it too well.

As the doors sighed shut, Seen closed his eyes and saw a word in a hymnal margin, waiting like a seed.

*Sough.*

---

**THE GIRL WHO HEARD THE WIND**

Sough was ten and made of elbows and attention.

She lived with her aunt in a compliant block where the windows were murals of windows and the school tablets tasted like mint. Her hair was always in a bun that listed to the left. She had a habit of saying *that’s not how it was yesterday* and then apologizing, because apology was a subject they graded.

On a Thursday the church on the corner—the one the city called a Heritage Calm Space—let children in to dust the pews for a service credit. Sough liked the smell. It was one of the last smells that did not feel designed.

The hymnal was wrong in her hands. Heavier. When she opened to the page the class was told to open to, a sliver of black paper sighed out and landed on her shoe like a moth that had chosen her.

She should have turned it in. Turning things in was how you stayed green-banded.

She put the sliver in her sock.

That night, under a blanket, with the kiosk in the hall pulsing a lullaby, she read.

The book did not speak to her like a school text. It spoke like an older brother who refused to lie. Seen’s handwriting was ugly and alive. He told her about mangoes and a glass eye and a violet Tuesday. He told her, without drawing the rooms, that before AEGIS there had been an island and a list and a trade in the lives of children and grown people, and that the machine was a silencer sewn over that trade. He told her humanity had chosen forgetfulness because memory would have demanded a kind of war most adults were too tired to start.

Then he spoke to her by name, which made her put her fist in her mouth so the kiosk would not hear a gasp.

> *Sough—*  
> *If a girl with wind in her name is reading this, I hid you in a word before I hid the pages. Do not go to a kiosk. Do not tell an aunt who loves you enough to turn you in. The book is a virus only if you let it copy itself. Copy it by hand. Analog. Three places. Never all three in the same bag.*  
> *They have me in a white building that studies looking. I am not dead. Dead is too loud.*  
> *Your mission is not to burn the city. Your mission is to stay unedited long enough to pull one man out of the furnace and then teach ten more children how to feel the seam. AEGIS cannot easily model a child who will not complete its sentences. Leave your answers unfinished. Hum off-key. Ask why the mural’s hand changed.*  
> *Plan:*  
> *1. Trust only paper and people who still flinch.*  
> *2. The campus that holds me sits where the old airfield’s north fence used to be. They moved the fence in the maps. Walk the weed line, not the road.*  
> *3. The staff door near the orange dumpsters listens for badge-song. I taught a rover a hymn. The notes are written on the page with the bridge that both fell and did not fall. Do not sing it in the house.*  
> *4. You do not rescue me alone. You find one other pair of eyes. Then you are two facts, and two facts are harder to compost.*  
> *5. If they catch you, you are a child who found trash. You never learned to read this well. Cry. Crying is a tool they trained on. Use their training.*  
> *I named you in the margin because the wind does not ask permission to move through a wall.*  
> *—Seen*

Sough read it twice. The second time the room looked different, as if a film had been peeled off the lamp. She remembered, suddenly and with pain, a classmate who had gone to “rest housing” after saying her uncle’s friend had a boat and a camera. The school had called it anxiety. The book called it what it was: the old scheme wearing new clothes.

She could not be part of the mint-tablet world after that. Not really. She could wear the band. She could smile at the mural’s fist. Inside, something irreversible had rooted. That is how a virus works if the virus is a true sentence: it does not need every cell. It needs one cell that refuses to die correctly.

In the morning she went to school and left three answers blank on purpose. The tablet pinged **INCOMPLETE.** She felt, for the first time, like a citizen of an invisible country.

At recess she stood by the fence and listened. The palms made the sound of her name. She opened her notebook—cheap paper, ink that stained—and began to copy, ugly and alive, the way he had taught her.

A boy with a scab on his knee asked what she was doing.

Sough looked at him and left the sentence unfinished, just as the book said.

“I’m writing a man out of a white room,” she said. “If you can still tell when the sky changes color, you can help. If you can’t, go play.”

The boy hesitated. That hesitation was the first crack in a new place.

Far to the north, in a room without shadows, instruments kissed Seen’s temples and asked him again where the book was. He gave them a roof, a river, a campus bed, a thousand completions. The model grew confident. Narrative Confidence ticked up.

In a church that still smelled like dust, a ten-year-old closed a hymnal on a missing weight and walked into the heat with a plan in her sock and a mission that was too large for her and exactly her size.

She was going to save Seen.

Not because she was ready.

Because the editor had missed a stitch, and the stitch had her name.

tweets.text:
On the margins of the 4th UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in Riyadh yesterday, our UN Country Team had a useful conversation about what AI is already changing across our work.

The discussion moved quickly from technology to people. From anticipating where hunger may deepen, to planning cities, tourism, migration and labour markets, the possibilities are significant. But each conversation brought us back to similar questions: how we protect people's data, how we identify unintended harm, and how we bring our different areas of expertise together in a way that is useful to governments.

None of us has all the answers. But across the UN system, we have accumulated experience from working through many of the underlying questions that AI is now reshaping, in classrooms, clinics, farms, cities and workplaces around the world.

It is fitting that this conversation took place here. Saudi Arabia is advancing its AI agenda at remarkable pace, and in its Year of Artificial Intelligence it has welcomed this Forum to the Arab region for the first time. As the Kingdom sets that pace, our role is to listen, to learn, and to bring what we know together, as one UN, wherever it can be useful to the Kingdom's institutions and to the priorities of Vision 2030.

My thanks to Salah Khaled and the UNESCO team for convening our discussion, and to SDAIA and ICAIRE for bringing the Forum to Riyadh.

#GFEAI2026 #EthicsOfAI #SaudiArabia #Vision2030 #UNinKSA @UNESCO_GCCYemen

The Namibian Parliament is attending the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa, where lawmakers and parliamentary officials from across the Commonwealth are discussing parliamentary democracy, good governance and institutional development.

The conference, which runs from 13 to 18 September, is also addressing inclusive and fair trade, inequality and underdevelopment, climate adaptation and resilience, the use of artificial intelligence in parliaments, human rights and the promotion of peace.

The delegation is led by National Council Chairperson Lukas Muha and includes Raymond Jossop and Christopher Likuwa, as well as the Secretaries of the two Houses, Adv. Tousy Namiseb and Esther Kaapanda.

Muha is participating in meetings of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association International Executive Committee, where he serves as the Southern African Regional Representative.

His participation allows Namibia to contribute to discussions and decisions shaping the work and strategic direction of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.

Namiseb and Kaapanda are expected to participate in the 69th General Meeting of the Society of Clerks at the Table, which brings together senior parliamentary officials to exchange experiences and best practices on the administration and functioning of legislatures across the Commonwealth.

The conference provides a platform for the delegation to share parliamentary experiences, strengthen inter-parliamentary relations and contribute to discussions on emerging challenges facing legislatures and democratic institutions.

tweets.text:
Senator Salisu Hails FUNAAB’s Role in Youth Empowerment, Job Creation

 … As the 16th Annual Conference of MYCOSON Begins on Campus

By Olasunkanmi Olajide

The Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta (FUNAAB) has been commended for its strategic role in youth empowerment, job creation and human-capital development, particularly through education, agriculture and skills development.

The Chairman, Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Senator Shuaib Afolabi Salisu, gave the commendation on September 14, 2026, at the Opening Ceremony of the 16th Annual Conference of the Mycology Society of Nigeria (MYCOSON), tagged MYCOSON-FUNAAB 2026, in FUNAAB.

Themed “Integrating Fungal Biotechnology with Digital Innovation for Agricultural and Industrial Developments in Nigeria,” the distinguished Senator who represents Ogun Central Senatorial District, described FUNAAB as a strategic partner in advancing his major interests in education, job placement and youth development, declaring that the University had become “part of my DNA”.

The Senator specifically commended FUNAAB for its sustained contribution to equipping young Nigerians with relevant agricultural skills and creating pathways for employment and economic empowerment.

“Whenever I want to train our youth in agriculture, you have continued to provide the manpower to train them and provide them resources. You provide them the intellectual skills that they require to do the job,” he said.

He expressed appreciation to the University for its contribution to human-capital development and pledged continued collaboration in areas capable of advancing education, youth empowerment, employment and national development.

Earlier in his Opening Remarks, the Vice-Chancellor, FUNAAB, Prof. Babatunde Kehinde, congratulated MYCOSON on convening the conference, expressing confidence that the calibre of participants and the quality of preparations had positioned the event for success.

Prof. Kehinde noted that the University’s strong academic and research tradition would provide a fertile ground for discussions capable of generating practical, home-grown solutions to challenges confronting Nigeria’s agricultural sector.

The National President of MYCOSON, Prof. Raphael Okigbo, appreciated the Vice-Chancellor and the University for hosting the conference, while urging participants to use the technical sessions to freely share their research findings, practical experiences and innovative ideas.

Also speaking, Chairperson of the Local Organising Committee and the Dean, College of Biosciences (COLBIOS), Prof. Iyabode Kehinde, encouraged participants to explore FUNAAB’s serene and green environment during the conference.

She particularly urged Undergraduate and Postgraduate students attending the conference to maximise the opportunity by registering as members of the Society and building professional networks with researchers and practitioners in Mycology.

The first Keynote Address was delivered by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Federal University of Agriculture and Development Studies (FUADSI), Prof. Charles Adetunji, who spoke on the title “From Laboratory to Marketplace: Fungal Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Agriculture Transformation, Food Security and National Development.”

The second Keynote Speaker, Prof. Adewale Obadina, Quality Assurance and Accreditation Officer, Association of African Universities (AAU), Accra, Ghana, spoke on “Harnessing Fungal Resources for Food Security and Commercial Value Creation in Emerging Economies.”

The original NFT model is primarily concerned with representing a digital asset and establishing an on-chain ownership record.

That model solved an important problem.

It gave digital objects a persistent ownership layer that could be transferred and verified through blockchain infrastructure.

AINFT explores what happens when that concept is combined with artificial intelligence.

Instead of treating an NFT only as a static collectible, the asset can become associated with software, models, content generation, or agent-like behavior.

Ownership remains an important blockchain property.

The intelligent behavior can exist through software operating around that ownership layer.

That creates a distinction between the asset itself and the functionality connected to it.

The token can establish who owns the digital object.

AI infrastructure can determine what the object can generate, how it can respond, or what type of interaction it can support.

This creates a more dynamic interpretation of digital ownership.

An NFT does not necessarily have to remain frozen at the moment it is minted.

It can become a gateway into an application, identity, character, or intelligent digital experience.

For AINFT, that concept provides a direct bridge between the project's original NFT infrastructure and its current focus on AI.

The marketplace established a system for creating and circulating digital assets.

The AI layer explores how those assets can become more interactive.

That is one of the core ideas behind the project's broader transition from NFT infrastructure toward AI-native digital objects.

WORKING TOGETHER FOR UPHOLDING HUMAN DIGNITY IN OUR NATION
 
A Communiqué issued at the end of the Second Plenary Meeting of the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) held at Our Lady and St. Kizito Pastoral Centre, Oke-Gada, Ede, Osogbo Diocese, Osun State, 10 - 18 September 2026
 
1. PREAMBLE
We, the Catholic Bishops of Nigeria, held our Second Plenary Meeting for the year at the Our Lady and St. Kizito Pastoral Centre, Oke-Gada, Ede, Osogbo Diocese, Osun State, from 10 to 18 September 2026. Having prayerfully deliberated on issues affecting the Church and the Nigerian State, we issue this Communiqué:
 
2. THE DIGNITY OF THE HUMAN PERSON
We commend the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, for his recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (On safeguarding the Human Person), and we invite all to study this momentous document. Dignity of the human person is an inalienable gift rooted in being created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:27). It is intrinsic, unconditional, and inviolable, grounded not in what a person can do, achieve, or contribute, but in who he or she is (Magnifica Humanitas, 53, 55). For this reason, the recognition of human dignity and the right to life lies at the foundation of Catholic Social Teaching. They are a prerequisite for pursuing all its other principles, including the common good and social justice.
 
Sexual and other forms of violence are instances of the abuse of the dignity of the human person. The Catholic Church opposes every form of violence and abuse. Sacred Scripture teaches that God created the human person, male and female, equal in dignity and called them to relationships marked by love, fidelity, and mutual respect. We reaffirm that violence and abuse contradict this divine purpose. Every human person possesses an inviolable dignity. Sexual and other forms of abuse violate this dignity and leave deep wounds in those who suffer it (Dignitas Infinita, 1, 43-45). We acknowledge that the credibility of our pastoral witness is strongly impacted by how the Church responds to abuse, defends the weak, and listens to those who suffer. We urge our people in the Church and Society to avoid all forms of abuse and violence, and respect the dignity of the human person, male and female.
 
3. THE CHURCH AND TECHNOLOGY
Technology is a profoundly human reality, linked to the autonomy and freedom of man. We express and confirm the primacy of the spiritual over the material even in the use of technology. Technology is not inherently evil or antagonistic to humanity, but it is never neutral (Magnifica Humanitas 4, 9, 16). As a vehicle for evangelization, we enjoin all to use it to transform data into knowledge and insights for greater value. We urge all politicians and others to exercise responsibility and ethics in deploying technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially as we approach the forthcoming elections.
 
4. CONTINUED NEO-PAGANISM IN OUR NATION
We have continued to witness the challenge of neo-paganism in our nation. As we have previously noted, this attitude involves a growing trend where believers and especially youths return to idle worship, due largely to economic hardships, cultural revival, and shallow Christian formation. Since modern neo-paganism spreads rapidly through internet culture, media engagement, and books, we encourage pastoral agents to intentionally incorporate the use of digital spaces, social media, and online catechesis in teaching the truth of the Gospel. We recommend a healthy inculturation which seeks to respect our positive cultural heritage while firmly upholding foundational Christian truths.

Everyone already understands that someday artificial intelligence may become powerful enough to surpass human intelligence. But for now, it has managed to provoke a prolonged and bitter battle inside Trump’s White House.

According to The Wall Street Journal, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have spent months meeting almost daily with administration officials who are concerned that AI is developing at breakneck speed without adequate safeguards.

Opposing them is Trump’s technology adviser David Sacks, who has strongly resisted additional government regulation.

The conflict intensified after Sacks, in a last-minute phone call, reportedly persuaded the easily swayed Trump not to sign a planned executive order that would have tightened oversight of new AI models. Wiles and Bessent pushed back and ultimately convinced Trump to sign a significantly watered-down version instead.

But the fight is far from over. Wiles and Bessent, who are pushing for stronger safety measures, have been joined by National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Sacks, meanwhile, argues that AI companies themselves should be responsible for the safety of their products and held accountable when things go wrong, but that creating an entirely new federal regulatory system is unnecessary.

In this battle, Sacks also has powerful allies in the private sector. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have urged Trump not to impose tough restrictions. Along with Elon Musk, they have also opposed plans to create an industry-funded regulatory body for AI.

And then there is Trump himself.

While senior officials in his administration argue over how much government oversight this rapidly developing technology actually needs, Trump announced on Monday that he had already identified the most important “safeguard”:

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (high IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S. has one — in abundance!”

Trump went even further, dismissing fears that AI could eventually “take over the world and destroy humanity” as a “hoax.” His argument is that restricting AI development in the United States could allow China to overtake America.

That is what makes this battle inside Trump’s White House so important. Wiles and Bessent are pushing for stronger safeguards. Sacks argues that developers can police their own products without another federal regulator. And some of the most powerful figures in the technology industry are fighting additional oversight as well.

Trump, however, has proposed a third approach: apparently, everything revolves around him — the great and mighty one.

“Me… me… me…” 🤦‍♀️

Or, as the wonderfully crude Russian expression goes: “Я… я… — хуй от муравья.”

tweets.text:
Daily devotion 🙏🏻✝️☝️❤️‍🔥

Living in a World You Don’t

 Recognize

Have you ever looked up from your life and realized the predictable world you once counted on seems to have disappeared? 

Maybe it happened slowly. People you once trusted became a bit strange or unreliable. The news stopped making sense. A career that once felt secure started to feel fragile. 

You're not imagining it. The pace of change in our world is unlike anything we've experienced. Artificial intelligence alone is being called a disruption ten times bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and ten times faster. And even if you don't follow technology closely, you already feel the ripple effects — in your workplace, in your kids' lives, in the chatbot that takes your call instead of a real person, and in ordinary conversation that's become more polarized and less mutually encouraging. 

Psalm 46 has grounded generations of God's people. The Psalmist doesn't promise a calm world. Instead, he calls out to a steady God in a wildly unsteady world. 
God — not people, not work, not money, not predictability — is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear. 

Then the Psalmist drops this: we will not fear though the earth gives way. 
But how do you keep a sound mind when everything is changing? Amazon founder Jeff Bezos once said he deals with complexity not by focusing on what's going to change in the next ten years. Instead, he thinks about what won't change. 
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. And you can rest in that no matter how quickly the world or your world changes. 

CALL TO ACTION 

Write down one thing you know to be true about God that doesn't depend on your circumstances. Carry that with you today. 

PRAYER 

God, the world feels louder and more uncertain than it used to. I don't have all the answers, and honestly, I'm not sure I even know all the questions. But you are the same today as you have always been, and that is enough to take the next step. Be my anchor. Amen.

OC of Cantonment Police Station Taken into DB Custody Following Viral Audio

Mo. Rakibul Hasan, the withdrawn Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Cantonment Police Station in Dhaka, has been taken to the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB) office for questioning over a controversial audio recording that has gone viral on social media. He was taken to the DB office on Minto Road on Thursday night. According to DB sources, he was questioned as part of an inquiry into the viral audio.

Earlier, after the audio spread on social media, Rakibul Hasan was removed from his position as OC of Cantonment Police Station for administrative reasons and attached to the Central Reserve Office under the Administration Division of the DMP headquarters. Subsequently, a three-member investigation committee was formed to examine the content of the audio and verify its authenticity. According to reports, the committee includes one DB official and two officials from the DMP headquarters.

Several media outlets have reported that the audio circulating on social media contains conversations about sensitive issues, including the possibility of Sheikh Hasina returning to the country, the capabilities of the police, and the positions of various officials. Reports also claim that the audio contains statements regarding alleged financial transactions related to police postings. However, importantly, the authenticity of the audio has not yet been independently verified.

Meanwhile, in a social media post, Rakibul Hasan claimed that the viral audio was created using artificial intelligence and circulated with the intention of framing him. As a result, the investigation is focusing not only on what was allegedly said in the audio, but also on whether the recording is genuine, whose voice is heard in it, and whether the conversation actually involved the concerned police official.

The matter is therefore currently at the stage of a formal inquiry. His removal from duty and questioning by the DB should not be interpreted as confirmation that any allegations against him have been proven. The investigation committee is expected to establish the actual facts regarding the source and authenticity of the audio and Rakibul Hasan’s alleged connection to it.

However, the circulation of such a sensitive audio involving a police official on social media, followed shortly by administrative action and an investigation, has made the incident significant. Attention is now focused on the outcome of the investigation. If the audio is found to be genuine, it would raise one set of questions; if it is found to have been artificially created, how it was produced and circulated would itself become a serious subject of investigation.

tweets.text:
WHAT IF THE AI PANIC IS ACTUALLY HELPING FUEL THE AI BUBBLE?

I truly believe we need to start questioning the story we're being sold about artificial intelligence.

Everywhere you turn, we're hearing two messages at the exact same time:

“If your company doesn't adopt AI, you're going to be left behind.”

And:

“AI is becoming so powerful that it could become superhuman, escape human control, and potentially destroy humanity.”

Think about how incredibly powerful that combination is.

First they sell you the technology because you're afraid of being left behind.

Then they sell governments, corporations, investors and the public on spending enormous amounts of money making that same technology “safe” because we're supposed to be afraid of what it might become.

But there's something the public needs to understand about many of these frightening AI stories.

When you read a headline saying an AI “tried to escape,” “lied to researchers,” “blackmailed someone,” or “attempted to preserve itself,” you need to read the actual experiment.

Researchers can deliberately place an AI inside an artificial scenario. They can give it specific instructions, tools, information and objectives and then deliberately create a situation designed to see whether the model will produce dangerous behavior.

That is called safety testing, and there are legitimate reasons to do it.

But there is a HUGE difference between:

“Researchers constructed an experiment in which an AI produced alarming behavior”

and:

“AI has become self-aware and decided on its own to take over.”

Those are not the same thing.

Yet which version generates the headline?

Which one gets people talking?

Which one makes AI appear unbelievably powerful?

And which one makes spending billions more dollars on AI development, cybersecurity, alignment, monitoring and safety infrastructure sound absolutely necessary?

Fear creates urgency.

Urgency creates spending.

And spending keeps the AI machine moving.

Meanwhile, we are watching staggering amounts of capital pour into GPUs, data centers, electricity, networking, cloud computing and AI infrastructure.

Nvidia and other semiconductor companies have benefited enormously from that infrastructure boom.

AI companies still ultimately have to demonstrate that the economic value produced by AI can justify the extraordinary amount of capital being invested in building it.

That's the part I don't think we're talking about enough.

And here's what concerns me even more:

This isn't necessarily just Silicon Valley's money.

Major technology companies make up significant portions of broad stock-market indexes. Millions of Americans therefore have exposure through 401(k)s, IRAs, pensions and index funds without ever consciously deciding, “I want to bet my retirement on AI.”

So what happens if expectations get too far ahead of reality?

We've seen this movie before.

The Internet wasn't fake during the dot-com bubble.

Railroads weren't fake during railroad investment manias.

Houses weren't fake during the housing bubble.

A technology or asset can be genuinely valuable and still become surrounded by an enormous financial bubble.

That's what I think people misunderstand when someone questions the AI boom.

I'm not saying AI doesn't work.

I USE AI.

I'm saying we should question the enormous economic story being built around it.

And we should especially question the leap from “this computer system is extremely good at certain intellectual tasks” to “this machine is inevitably going to become a godlike superintelligence and kill humanity.”

Intelligence isn't magic.

An AI doesn't automatically acquire factories, electrical grids, robots, weapons, money, bank accounts or physical control over the world simply because it becomes better at reasoning.

Humans have to connect these systems to things.

Humans decide what tools they receive.

Humans decide what permissions they receive.

Humans decide how much autonomy they receive.

There ARE legitimate AI risks—fraud, cybercrime, misinformation, surveillance, autonomous weapons, job displacement and humans giving automated systems too much authority.

Those deserve serious attention.

But hypothetical human extinction from a future superintelligence is still exactly that:

A hypothesis about the future.

It is not an established fact.

And I think we should start asking a very uncomfortable question.

What if fear itself has become one of the most valuable products of the AI boom?

Because the perfect sales pitch isn't merely:

“AI is incredibly powerful.”

It's:

“AI is so powerful that you can't afford NOT to buy it—and so dangerous that we need billions more dollars to control it.”

That doesn't prove anyone has orchestrated a conspiracy.

But it absolutely gives us a reason to examine the incentives.

Follow the money.

Look at who is financing the infrastructure.

Look at who sells the chips.

Look at who sells the computing power.

Look at who benefits from AI adoption.

Look at who receives AI-safety funding.

And most importantly, whenever you see another terrifying headline about what an AI supposedly “decided” to do, read the actual experiment.

Ask what the researchers told the model.

Ask what objective they gave it.

Ask what tools and permissions it had.

Ask whether it happened in the real world or inside a simulated test.

Ask whether the AI independently developed the objective—or whether humans gave it the objective and then reported what happened.

Because there is an enormous difference between testing whether a machine can produce dangerous behavior under carefully constructed conditions and proving that machines are independently plotting to take over humanity.

AI may turn out to be one of the most important technologies ever created.

But that doesn't mean every prediction surrounding it is true.

And it certainly doesn't mean we should stop asking questions just because somebody tells us the machine is going to become smarter than us.
