From healthcare to finance, its applications are vast and varied.

This could revolutionize how we approach education.

In the creative industries, AI is also making waves.

While some fear that AI might replace human jobs, it is more likely to augment our capabilities.

By automating repetitive tasks, AI allows us to focus on more complex and creative endeavors.

However, ethical considerations surrounding AI cannot be overlooked.

Ensuring that AI is used responsibly and without bias is crucial.

As we continue to develop this technology, collaboration between technologists, ethicists, and policymakers is essential.

Building AI solutions requires a blend of data science, programming, and domain expertise.

For those interested in diving into AI, starting with online courses can be a great first step.

Platforms like Coursera and edX offer numerous resources to learn the basics.

Engaging in hands-on projects can also boost your skills and understanding.

As AI continues to evolve, staying informed about the latest trends and developments is vital.

The future of AI holds incredible potential, and we are just beginning to scratch the surface.

The original posting required only a high school diploma. But after Andrew applied, the qualification was changed to require graduation from an "accredited" school, meaning homeschoolers need not apply.

Startup Develops Remedies For Future AI Bioweapons

"In a wine bar near OpenAI’s office in San Francisco, biotech entrepreneurs Hannu Rajaniemi and Nikolai Eroshenko were worried—and excited.

Fast advances in artificial intelligence were threatening to make it possible for terrorists or rogue states to develop deadly new bioweapons.

Now their AI biosecurity startup, called Red Queen Bio, is rushing to design antibodies that can be manufactured to protect against a range of potential pathogens, including the seemingly sci-fi threat of an AI-designed virus.

As AI capabilities increase and incidents with rogue AI systems proliferate, fears are mounting that AI could destroy civilization.

While some skeptics say the danger of AI bioweapons is overblown, big AI developers say risks from their tools are increasing. OpenAI last year observed hundreds of users asking their chatbot how to make and deploy poisons and biological weapons, including aerosolized pathogens and modified measles.

Anthropic this month said it had detected attempts to use its Claude chatbot to engineer a dangerous bird flu adapted for mammals, with 'enhanced pandemic potential.' Queries from a Claude user affiliated with a military research institute asked about ways to make the chikungunya virus more harmful. Another user asked Anthropic’s chatbot questions about viruses related to smallpox.

Aspects of the dynamics of biological warfare favor attackers over defenders, said Olivia Scharfman, a biotech fellow at the Institute for Progress, a think tank that has received funding from Open Philanthropy, now called Coefficient Giving, one of the biggest backers of AI safety initiatives.

'Attackers have as long as they want to develop a bioweapon. We don’t have years to design a countermeasure,' Scharfman said.

The company belongs to an emerging industry of biosecurity startups in the AI era. Two Anthropic leaders invested in Pilgrim, a startup backed by Peter Thiel that is developing hardware to detect viruses in the air."

By Georgia Wells

Neuroscience versus artificial intelligence 

You want to know how lame AI vision systems are compared to humans?

Almost everyone who has seen pictures of Abraham Lincoln will recognize this image almost instantly. This is true even if they're seeing it for the first time.

A deep neural net, on the other hand, will fail to recognize the image unless it has been specifically trained to recognize it.

Why is that, you ask? It is because recognition in the brain is based on a winner-take-all mechanism that is extremely tolerant of noise and distortions. By contrast, a deep learning system is based on the statistics of connection weights. Yep, DL sucks. 😀
